Decided now rather than at Stage 4 because the seam it constrains is how a backend is BUILT, and Stage 2's codebook net lands first: a net constructible only by cloning a warmed instance would be discovered as a design error a whole stage late — flips if a backend appears whose per-position state is genuinely immutable, which would still get its own instance per thread and simply not care.

D-113: A candidate radius of 9 through 64 is provably equivalent to 8, so running a radius experiment above 8 is an experiment-design error and not a config error — the candidate set is the policy's ball INTERSECTED with pistol-core's own legality answer, asked one cell at a time (D-77), and the rule-5 legal region is the union of radius-8 balls around the stones (rule 5, D-101); a policy ball of radius at least 8 centred on a stone therefore already contains that stone's whole legal ball, and the intersection discards everything beyond it. Every radius in 9..64 yields the identical candidate set, the identical tree and the identical move, and `MAX_CANDIDATE_RADIUS` stays what D-18 calls a rejection bound — a statement about what a document may say, not about what plays differently. Two things are deliberately NOT done. No validation change refusing radius > 8: that check would have to import the rules' constant into config validation, which is the conflation CLAUDE.md rule 2 names outright and D-20 exists to prevent, and the cost of the error it would catch is a wasted experiment rather than a wrong move. No enumeration of the equivalent range in the schema either: the radius policy is scheduled for supersession by Stage 1's threat-first staged generator (D-52, D-79, ROADMAP WP-1.5), and pinning a table against a policy with a known expiry is work that expires with it — flips if the radius policy outlives Stage 1 as the primary candidate source, at which point the equivalence is worth one comment in the config document itself.

D-114: The flamegraph session is pre-registered with exactly two hypotheses and adjudicates BEFORE any fix (CLAUDE.md rule 5's no-post-hoc-thresholds, applied to profiling): H1 = the eval apply/undo pair per candidate per node in move ordering; H2 = per-node allocation in `candidates.rs`/`ordering.rs`, each of which builds a fresh `Vec` at every node. This amends D-76's letter: that line calls the roundtrip "this work package's registered hotspot and the first thing a Stage-1 bench should attack", which registered it on reasoning alone and left no room for a competing explanation of the same cost — H1 is that same suspicion, now stated as a hypothesis a profile can refute rather than a conclusion a bench merely quantifies. The profile is operator hardware, a release build, instrument mode, and fixed-NODE runs at two stone counts — nodes and not movetime, because D-95 makes a movetime budget a floor plus one uninterruptible first iteration and would profile that instead of the search; two stone counts, because D-95's own measurement shows candidate-set cost grows with how far apart the stones sit, so a single opening profile would understate H2 by construction. Whatever the profile confirms then earns its own rule-5 pre-registered bench with a hotspot, an expected gain bracket and an abort threshold: the profile chooses the target and the bench judges the fix, and neither is allowed to do the other's job. The session runs on the operator's machine as ROADMAP WP-1.3 — flips never; a third hypothesis means a new line here and a new profile, never an addition to this one after the numbers are in.

D-115: In-source `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` blocks are PERMITTED, for pinning private invariant guards only — behaviour-level pinning stays in the behaviour-named integration suites under `tests/` (CLAUDE.md rule 7), and no item is made public, no `pub(crate)` is widened and no signature is altered to let a test reach it. The gap this closes is real: a guard whose removal is invisible from outside the crate cannot be pinned from outside the crate, and the only alternative on offer was to widen the surface, which trades a permanent API for a test. Two such guards land with this line. `ordering::tests::a_table_move_that_is_not_a_candidate_is_dropped_rather_than_played`: a 64-bit verification word can in principle answer about a different position (D-8), so the table's move is not necessarily a candidate here, and promoting one anyway would place a stone the policy never offered — surfacing a level down as `CANDIDATE_ILLEGAL`, naming the policy for something the ordering did. `pv::tests::a_cleared_line_is_not_adopted_by_the_parent_that_promotes_over_it`: `clear` drops the length and leaves the coordinates where they are, so the length is the entire guard against a parent adopting a previous sibling's line and reporting a variation it never searched. Each was mutation-checked — the guard removed, the test observed red, the guard restored — and each names the mutation it was checked against in its own doc comment, because a guard test never seen to fail pins nothing, which is D-55's and D-60's argument about a value copied out of the code it checks — flips if an in-source module starts pinning behaviour rather than an invariant, which is evidence the behaviour has no home in `tests/` and the crate seam is in the wrong place.

D-116: A reviewer finding is verified with a minimal reproducer before its fix lands, and a finding that cannot be reproduced is recorded as REJECTED together with the reproducer that was attempted — codifying the R3 episode. A review is worth having precisely because it is written without the implementer's assumptions, which is the same reason a review can be confidently wrong about a path it never ran; a reproducer is the cheapest thing that separates the two cases, and writing one is bounded work where chasing a speculative fix is not. The rejected half matters as much as the verified half, and therefore needs somewhere durable to live: a rejection that would change a reader's model of the system goes in THIS file as its own line, and the rest stays in the work package's review record — because a rejection recorded only in an ephemeral review report does not reach the next reviewer, which is the whole failure it exists to prevent. D-101 is the precedent and the shape: a question asked, answered against the platform spec, and written down here with what a demotion would have cost, so nobody re-derives it. The amendment is one sentence in CLAUDE.md's Process section, beside D-99's — flips never; a finding whose reproducer would itself be a work package is still recorded, as a finding with its reproducer named rather than written.

D-117: The Stage-1 work-package cut of record is WP-1.1 search oracle -> WP-1.2 minimal arena -> WP-1.3 calibration experiments -> WP-1.4 movetime-ceiling fix -> WP-1.5 threat infrastructure -> WP-1.6 threat-only zone-bounded quiescence -> WP-1.7 killers/history/countermove on pair moves -> WP-1.8 AND-OR solver and relevance-zone Deep df-pn (+1+epsilon, GHI), written out in docs/ROADMAP.md's Stage-1 section, whose previous ordering this supersedes. Two things moved and both for the same reason. The differential search oracle (D-106) goes FIRST, ahead of the arena: it makes no strength claim and so needs no judge, while everything after it is a pruning change that SPRT judges for strength and not for soundness — a pruning commit that quietly changed the value of the tree would pass an SPRT, so the soundness reference has to predate the first pruner rather than merely predate the threat machinery. The arena lands second and is what every WP after it is measured by (CLAUDE.md rule 6). The rest is dependency order made explicit: calibration (r=2 vs r=3 fixed-node paired SPRT with its verdict pre-registered, the decided-window floor experiment D-105 keeping its pre-registered home there because it is an arena experiment too, and D-114's profile) needs the arena to exist; the movetime-ceiling fix (D-95) is play-mode only and blocks nothing, so it sits ahead of the threat work rather than behind it, where a forfeit risk should not wait; threat infrastructure — window-count and hot-window tables, the must-block filter, the unblockable-double-threat check, the mechanisms docs/research/sealbot_notes.md measures working in another engine for this exact game — is the data structure quiescence needs and therefore precedes it; quiescence is bound by D-111; and killers, history and countermove are ordering changes worth measuring only once the candidate set they order is the threat-first one. The countermove is named explicitly because the research report's Stage-1 line and `ordering.rs`'s own module doc both promise it, and a compressed restatement that dropped it would have been the silent drift rule 10 forbids. Each WP gets its own prompt and names its gates there — flips per WP: a cut that moves is an amendment on this line, never a silent reorder of the ROADMAP.

D-118: `crates/pistol-search/src/pvs.rs` is the first file to exceed CLAUDE.md rule 9's soft cap; it carries its why-justification in its own module doc (stating no count, as the rule requires), and the file-justification GATE stays unmechanized. This is recorded here because the choice was otherwise stated only in a `tools/ci.sh` echo — which is the silent architecture drift rule 10 forbids, and which that echo itself said needed a line here. The justification: `visit` is one recursion whose parts are not independent — the window a child inherits depends on whether the ply was the mover's second stone or the opponent's reply, the table's bound depends on the alpha the node started with, the abort path must unwind through every one of them without a result being used, and the invariants that make it correct (the mate re-basing D-72 fixes, D-78's no-cutoff-at-a-PV-node rule, the two horizons of D-111) are stated against the whole. Splitting it would pass six values between free functions and put the reasoning in a different file from the code it constrains, which is a worse read for a smaller number. The honest reduction is scheduled rather than forced: Stage 1 moves candidate generation out of this file entirely (D-117, WP-1.5). The gate is not mechanized because a check has to RECOGNIZE a justification, which means a marker convention that every future justified file must carry, and inventing a workspace-wide convention to police one file is a schema decision taken at the worst moment to take it; `tools/ci.sh` therefore reports the gate as OWED rather than as having nothing to run, which is the honest state rather than the skip-with-default rule 3 forbids — flips when a second file crosses the cap, which is when the convention is worth designing and is what this line is waiting for.

---

D-119: What the differential search oracle asserts, in three parts, because "the search agrees with the reference" is three different claims. (1) About the MOVE, only that it is in the reference's ARGMAX SET — never identity. Among equal-scoring turns the engine's pick IS its move-ordering pass, which the reference deliberately does not have, so pinning the move would pin the ordering rather than the value, and a Stage-4 retune would read as a soundness failure; WHICH tie the engine takes is pinned already, by the cross-process determinism gate (D-7), and ties are the normal case rather than the exception. (2) About the SCORE, that it agrees once CLASSIFIED, with the reference carrying its own three-band `WinInTurns`/`Value`/`LossInTurns` built from turn arithmetic alone and the test mapping `classify`'s answer onto it — a reference that built its mate scores with the crate's own `mate_in` would cancel an error in `MATE`, in `mate_in` or in `classify` against itself, and exact mate distances are precisely what the work package asks this oracle to certify, so D-3's packing has to be under test rather than assumed. (3) About the LINE, that a claimed mate actually arrives — on both sides of the band, a claimed win and a claimed loss alike, by the side the score says wins and on the turn the distance names — replayed through `GameState::make_turn` and not by placing a canonical pair in canonical order, which D-51 says is not always the playable ordering. The third part exists because (1) and (2) look only at the ROOT turn, so a principal variation whose tail is not the line the score was proved on passes both, which is what D-78 exists to prevent and what the determinism gate cannot see because it compares two runs of the same engine. The expensive half of that — every prefix position's reference value under D-72's parity — is deliberately not bought — flips if the reference ever gains an ordering pass, at which point move identity becomes assertable and would say something.

D-120: The oracle's depth ceiling and runtime budget, measured before the matrix was chosen rather than discovered after (CLAUDE.md rule 5). Full-width per-TURN branching in this game is about C-squared where C is the candidate count, and C is at least 6 in the smallest position that exists (one stone, radius 1): measured on that position at radius 1, a reference run costs 49 nodes at depth 1, 5 377 at depth 2, 999 841 at depth 3 (2.3 s release) and 273 594 001 at depth 4 (614 s, measured and not extrapolated). So the suite splits in two, the way `perft_tests.rs` splits for the same reason (D-54): `search_oracle_tests.rs` carries what a debug build can afford on every commit, against a pre-registered ceiling of 5 s debug on the development machine (measured: 3.95 s and 1.85 s for its two binaries, which grew the workspace test run from 83 s to 89 s), and `search_oracle_deep_tests.rs` carries the third turn, is `#[ignore]`d, and is run in release by `tools/search_oracle_check.sh` as CI gate 10 (measured: 84.4 s, with the whole gate 86 s). Depth 4 is NOT run at any radius, and that is the number above rather than a judgement. Two consequences are recorded because they are not obvious. The exact mate distance of three costs 37 050 968 reference nodes (84 s) on a purpose-built eleven-stone position, and that is a floor rather than a fixture choice: a forced mate in three needs a double four after the mover's turn, which needs seven own stones and therefore five before it, which with P1's always-odd stone count fixes the position at eleven stones, and fifteen candidates at radius 1 is the packing floor for eleven stones. And the reference enumerates BOTH orderings of every pair at every interior node, as the engine's ply-level recursion does (D-79); evaluating each unordered turn once instead is exact and measured 3.9x cheaper at depth 3 on the opening (999 841 nodes against 255 418) and 6.75x at depth 4 (273 594 001 against 40 535 269), which would have brought the mate-in-three case to roughly fifteen seconds and made depth 4 affordable on one position — and it is declined, because it would change a method the work package pre-registered in order to hit a budget, because the dedupe key has to carry rule 4's truncation (the pair {a,b} whose smaller cell wins is realised by one ordering only) and the reference is the one component here that must have no correctness argument of its own, and because the two orderings agreeing is D-79's premise and one of the three arguments D-106 built this oracle to certify — flips if the release gate's runtime becomes the thing that stops it being run, in which case the dedupe is the change to make and this line records what it costs and what it gives up.

D-121: The table-size independence check asserts that the SCORE does not move and that every size still plays a turn the reference rates best; it does NOT assert that the MOVE is the same. D-109 measured that move choice is not invariant under table size — two turns that tie on score are separated by whichever the ordering tried first, the table's move goes first, so table contents decide the tie — so a test pinning move identity would pin a property this project has already recorded as false, and would be a time bomb rather than a gate. Pinning it "only where it empirically holds" would be worse: that is a threshold chosen after the numbers are in, which the Process section forbids outright. The sizes run are 96 bytes, 1 MiB and 256 MiB — the first being the smallest table the type can build rather than the smallest a config may state (D-19's `MIN_TT_BYTES` binds documents, not `Table::new`), because one bucket is maximum collision pressure and that is where a 64-bit verification word (D-8) would show, and it is what D-109's own measurement used. What the one-bucket size deliberately does NOT cover, because an earlier draft of this line claimed it did and both reviews disproved it with the same reproducer: the table's mate re-basing (D-72). Replacing `score::shift` with the identity leaves every one of the oracle's assertions green at every table size and every depth, and is caught immediately by `tt_tests::tt_mate_score_depth_adjustment_roundtrips`. The reason is structural and no fixture or size fixes it — within one search from one root, `turns_from_root` is a function of the key (the stone count fixes the turn, the phase and the mover together, D-58), so every probe re-bases by exactly the amount it was stored with and the conversion is provably a no-op; the re-basing only matters for a table that survives into a search from a DIFFERENT root, and this oracle builds a fresh `Searcher` per run precisely so that a carried table is not an input to the answer (D-109). That property is real and it is pinned in `tt_tests`, one crate-local unit away, not here — flips never; the score not depending on the table is the soundness claim this oracle exists to make, and the move not depending on it is not a claim anyone made.

D-122: The oracle reads `crates/pistol-cli/tests/fixtures/tactical_v0.txt` and `crates/pistol-core/tests/fixtures/perft_positions_v1.txt` in place, from pistol-search's test tree, and does NOT re-pin their SHA-256s. D-37 pins a fixture in the test that reads it because a fixture carries GOLDEN VALUES, and editing the file without editing the expectation must be a red test; this suite carries no golden values at all — its expectation is agreement between two implementations, which is invariant under every edit to the position set — so a third std-only SHA-256 in the workspace would pin a file whose contents cannot change this suite's verdict, and drift is still caught by the owning crates' own pins in the same `cargo test --workspace` run. What this does create is an undeclared cross-crate coupling: moving or renaming either fixture breaks a test in a crate that does not own it, with no compile-time signal, and the strict readers in `tests/common/fixture_text.rs` know both grammars, so a new directive in either file is a loud failure here as well as there. That is the cost, it is named rather than argued away, and it is cheaper than either a third hashing copy or a ninth crate to hold one — flips if a third crate needs to read the same fixtures, at which point the loaders and the pin earn a home together rather than a third copy each.

D-123: The oracle compares the engine's answer at the depth its iterative deepening STOPPED at against the reference's answer at the depth that was REQUESTED, and that is sound only while the search is full-width. `search.rs` breaks out of the deepening loop on `is_mate(score)`, so a position with a mate in one is answered from the first iteration however deep the budget was; the comparison still holds because in a full-width search a mate score at the root is EXACT — a proven win ends the game, a proven loss requires every root turn to be one, and any shorter mate would already have been inside the horizon that found the longer one, so neither the fact nor the distance moves with more depth. The three mate-in-one cases kept at depth 2 in the release tier are there for exactly this: they are the only runs where the engine answers from a depth other than the one the reference searched, and their agreement is what makes every other depth comparison in the suite mean what it says. This is written down rather than left in the argument because its premise is the thing Stage 1 exists to remove: the first forward-pruning or reducing change makes "mate found at depth d" no longer exact, and the oracle must then either compare at the depth the engine reports or have this argument made again — flips with WP-1.5 and whatever it prunes, which is the same day this line becomes the reason a comparison basis has to change.

D-124: A value-differential oracle cannot see a search that narrows its candidate set at the TAIL, and that is a limit of the method rather than of this matrix. Verified with a reproducer before being written down (D-116): dropping the worst-ordered candidate at every node of `pvs::visit` — one `cells.pop()` after `order` — leaves every one of the oracle's assertions green, all ten always-on tests and all three release ones, across 31 fixtures, three depths, two radii and three table sizes; dropping the BEST-ordered candidate instead turns six of the ten red at once, naming the fixture and the move, and an off-by-one in the engine's mate distance turns two red. The reason is structural and no fixture fixes it: the oracle compares VALUES, the dropped turn is the one move ordering rated worst, and a turn that is never the argmax cannot move a maximum however deep it is searched — a wider fixture set or a fourth turn would not help, because the mutation is invisible by construction. What would help is comparing the engine's per-node candidate set with the reference's, which needs visibility into `pvs` that this work package's non-goals forbid (no new public surface, and D-115 permits an in-source test only for a private invariant, not for a cross-crate comparison). This is recorded because Stage 1's very next candidate-set change is exactly this shape: WP-1.5's threat-first staged generation supersedes the radius policy with DOMINANCE PRUNING, which is a rule for dropping moves it rates worse (D-52, D-79). So the work package that lands it inherits the fact that this oracle will not judge its dominance rule, and owes a check of its own — flips when that check lands, which is where the visibility question gets settled.

D-125: The oracle's soundness claim about the SEARCH WINDOW rests on exactly one comparison, and it is named here so that nobody cheapens the gate by dropping it. Found independently by both reviews, each with its own reproducer: deleting the re-search in `pvs::child` — so that a null-window scan which fails high is returned as the node's value — and making the transposition cutoff unconditional — any bound, any depth, principal-variation nodes included, in breach of D-78 — are each invisible to EVERY always-on assertion, over 31 fixtures at two radii, three table sizes and two turns, and invisible as well to the release tier's depth-2 breadth over eighteen fixtures and to the 37-million-node mate-in-three case. The one comparison that catches either is `tight_cluster_at_a_turn_boundary` at depth 3 and radius 1, 9 308 846 reference nodes and about 21 s: engine `Value(780)` against reference `Value(910)` for the deleted re-search, and `Value(332)` against `Value(910)` for the unconditional cutoff. That is structural rather than a fixture gap — at two turns the sub-search below a null-window scan is shallow enough that the window returns the exact value, so no width, radius or table size at depth 2 can see a window bug. Two things follow. The gate's cost is not where its power is: about 84 of its 85 seconds are the mate-in-three case, which buys the only exact mate distance above two and catches NEITHER window bug, while the 21 s case carries the window claim alone — so a future trim of the gate must know which second is which. And every commit between gate runs is covered by a tier that cannot see a window bug at all, which is a consequence of the debug budget (D-120) rather than of the method: unlike D-124's blindness, a depth-3 comparison does close this one — flips if a depth-3 comparison ever becomes affordable in a debug build, which is the day the always-on tier can carry this claim itself.

D-126: Takes D-120's own flip clause, operator-approved: the reference values each unordered turn ONCE, and both-orderings enumeration survives as a mode with exactly one caller. D-120 declined the dedupe on three grounds and two of them are now paid for rather than argued away. The dedupe key is the `Turn` and not the cell set, so rule 4's truncation is carried and not merged — a first stone that completes a line makes a ONE-stone turn, enumerates no pair, and therefore never suppresses the other ordering of a pair it belongs to, which is the one ordering that pair has; the skip test is membership in a per-node ledger of first stones whose ply CONTINUED the turn, and the argument that this is exact in both directions is stated against the ledger in `tests/common/pair_dedupe.rs`. D-79's premise — the two orderings of a pair are worth the same at search depth — was the third ground and it keeps a check rather than losing one: `reference_dedupe_matches_both_orderings_enumeration` runs both modes over four fixtures at the depths a debug build affords and compares the whole per-turn map, `reference_dedupe_matches_both_orderings_below_the_root` does the same at two turns in the release tier where rule 4 truncates at an INTERIOR node, and `dedupe_keeps_the_pair_whose_ordering_rule_4_truncates` asserts the shape directly so that two modes agreeing by both losing a turn is still red. Verified by mutation in a separate worktree, never the live tree, before this line was written (D-116): keying the dedupe on the cell set instead of the turn turns the first and third red, dedupe by ascending order alone without the membership test turns those two red plus the movegen cross-check, and reversing the interior candidate loop fires `REFERENCE_DEDUPE_KEY_UNSORTED` by name. The re-measured numbers, which supersede D-120's: tier-1 1.74 s and 1.50 s debug against a 5 s budget (was 3.95 s and 1.85 s), the workspace test run 86.6 s (was 89 s), the release gate 19.6 s (was 86 s), its deep tier 18.1 s (was 84.4 s), the mate-in-three case at depth 3 6 714 383 reference nodes and 18.0 s run alone (was 37 050 968 and 84 s), and `tight_cluster_at_a_turn_boundary` at depth 3 — the one comparison that carries D-125's window claim — 1 879 674 nodes (was 9 308 846). The gate-shape question D-120 left open is closed by the pre-registered rule the operator set before the measurement: at 18.0 s the mate-in-three case is under the 35 s that would have re-opened the cut, so the gate keeps its shape. And a fourth turn is now affordable and is added, on the cheapest position that can carry one: `empty_board_turn_1` at depth 4 is 255 419 reference nodes and 1.4 s, because an empty board offers the policy one cell and the tree below the opening stone is `one_stone_at_the_origin`'s depth-3 tree — what it buys is on the ENGINE's side, seven plies of `plies_for` over rule 3's one-stone opening turn plus three pair turns, one turn past anything else in the suite. The next cheapest depth-4 case is that position's own at 40 535 269 deduped nodes, which is minutes, and it stays out — flips if a reference-side bug is ever traced to the dedupe, in which case `PairOrder::BothOrderings` is one argument away and the mode comparison is what would have caught it.

D-127: `[profile.release] overflow-checks = true`, operator ruling, amending D-14's letter and not its reason. D-14 defers `[profile.release]` settings because codegen tuning is a perf-sensitive change and CLAUDE.md rule 5 wants a pre-registered hotspot and an IQR-gated bench before one lands; this is not codegen tuning, it is which CHECKS the shipping build keeps, and the thing it prevents is the one class of error a rule-3 fail-loud project cannot otherwise catch — a wrapped i16 coordinate or a wrapped turn count is not a crash, it is a legal-looking wrong answer the engine goes on to play, and in release Rust wraps it silently. D-34 and D-44 already require checked arithmetic wherever a coordinate is computed by hand; this closes the same hole for arithmetic nobody wrote a `checked_*` for, including whatever a future contributor writes. Its cost was measured rather than assumed, because rule 5's spirit applies even where its bench harness does not exist yet (`bench` is still unimplemented, D-14): fixed-NODE runs of 2 000 896 nodes under `configs/instrument_v0.toml`, five repetitions each, median nps 206 925 -> 204 325 on the one-stone opening and 167 178 -> 165 276 on the quiet midgame position — 1.3% and 1.1%, against a 0.5 s design point that is nowhere near tight enough for that to buy anything. It is pinned by `bare_integer_overflow_panics_under_this_profile`, which runs in the release pass of `tools/search_oracle_check.sh` because a debug build has overflow checks by default and would pass the test without asserting anything; verified by mutation in a separate worktree before this line was written (D-116), where deleting the flag turns that test red in release and nothing else in the workspace notices — flips if a profile shows the check inside a hot loop that a `checked_*` with a named panic would state better, which is a code change and not a profile change.

D-128: `[profile.release-checked]`, inheriting release and adding `debug-assertions = true`, operator ruling. It is the profile red-team and deep-verification runs build, and it exists so that nobody edits an assertion's CLASS to go looking for something: the alternative that was actually happening is hand-hardening a `debug_assert!` into an `assert!` for one investigation and hand-reverting it after, which is a source edit whose only record is that somebody remembered to undo it. Measured shape of the three profiles, so the claim is a run and not a reading of `Cargo.toml`: dev has debug assertions on and overflow checks on, release has debug assertions off and overflow checks on (D-127), release-checked has both on at release optimization. Nothing in CI runs it, deliberately — it is an instrument, not a gate, and a gate that ran it would double every release gate's build for checks the deployment build does not keep — flips if a `debug_assert!` ever guards something a gate must see, which would mean it was misclassified under D-129 rather than that this profile needs a gate.

D-129: The assertion taxonomy, operator ruling, stated so that the choice between the two macros stops being a judgement call made twice. `assert!` = a CORRECTNESS invariant, active in every profile: something whose violation makes the answer wrong rather than merely suspicious — transposition-table field ranges, the desync guards in `Position`, `GameState` and `pv`, coordinate overflow, and a candidate policy that runs dry half way through a turn. `debug_assert!` = a DIAGNOSTIC whose cost is unwanted on the deployment hot path: a statement that is true by construction and is asserted because a future extension could break the construction, sitting somewhere that runs per node or per leaf — `STATIC_EVAL_MID_TURN` at the depth-0 horizon is the case the rule was written from (D-111), and D-128's profile is where it is live. A compile-time `const` assertion is outside the taxonomy entirely: it is a build error, not a runtime class. The existing assertions were audited against this and NOT ONE was reclassified, which is the honest outcome and is recorded because a taxonomy that changed nothing looks unmotivated otherwise: the workspace has exactly one `debug_assert!` and it is the exemplar the definition names, and every other runtime assertion guards a wrong answer rather than a suspicion — flips if a correctness invariant is ever measured to cost enough to matter, which is a rule-5 bench and a named exception on this line, never a quiet demotion.

D-130: A review is dispatched against a NAMED REVISION and mutation testing runs in a separate git WORKTREE, never the live tree — operator ruling, amending CLAUDE.md's Process section beside D-99's and D-116's sentences. Both halves close a way for a review to be about nothing. A reviewer reading "the working tree" reads whatever the implementing session happens to have saved at the moment it looks, so a finding can name a line that no longer exists and a clean verdict can certify code that was replaced while it was being read; naming the revision costs one `git stash create` where the work is uncommitted, and a report header that states the revision and whether HEAD still matches it makes a stale review say so instead of looking current. Mutation testing has the sharper failure: a mutation is a deliberate break, and a deliberate break sitting in the tree the implementer is editing is indistinguishable from a regression — worse, an interrupted mutation run leaves it there, and the next gate to go red is diagnosed against a file nobody meant to change. A worktree is the cheapest isolation `git` already has, it shares the object store so it costs a checkout rather than a clone, and `git worktree remove --force` is one command. This session applied the rule to itself: D-126's dedupe and D-127's profile flag were both mutation-verified in worktrees at named revisions, and the REVIEW-impl over them was dispatched against a stash-create SHA — flips never; a harness that could pin a revision another way is this rule under a different name.

D-131: CLAUDE.md rule 9's file-justification gate is mechanized as `tools/file_justification_check.sh`, CI gate 11, taking D-118's flip clause — a second file crossed the cap, which is what that line said it was waiting for. The convention D-118 declined to invent, now that there is more than one file to police: the cap is **300 lines**, which is what "~300-line soft cap" is worth as a number a script can compare; over it is not a failure but a demand for a sentence; and the sentence is a comment line carrying `RULE9-JUSTIFICATION:` followed by the why on that same line. The marker goes in the module doc where the argument already lives rather than in a pragma, because a checker has to RECOGNIZE a justification and prose cannot be recognized, and because the reader who needs the why is reading the top of the file. Rule 9's other half — counts are derived, never asserted — is checked too: a why with a numeral beside "line" or "lines" fails. That check catches the literal form and not a count spelled out in words, and the script says so about itself rather than implying a proof. The gate self-tests before it runs, over five seeded files in a temporary directory, one per verdict: a checker nobody has watched fail is not a checker, and this one is mostly asked to say "no" about files that do not exist yet. Landing it found the second violation immediately and it was this session's own: `search_oracle_universe_tests.rs` had grown to 327 lines under D-126, and the honest answer there was a split rather than a sentence — the dedupe equivalence tests are the reference checking ITSELF, which is neither an agreement assertion nor a universe one, so they moved to `search_oracle_dedupe_tests.rs` and the gate script runs the third binary. `pvs.rs` keeps its argument unchanged and gains the marker on its heading — flips if a third file needs a justification whose why does not fit one line, which would make the marker a block convention rather than a line one, and is a change to the checker rather than to the rule.

D-132: Amends D-118's second half, which said the file-justification gate stays unmechanized and that `tools/ci.sh` would report it as OWED. It is mechanized (D-131) and the OWED line is deleted from `ci.sh`, which is the point of having written the deferral down: D-118 named its own flip condition — a second file crossing the cap — and that is what happened, in the very next work package, for the reason D-118 anticipated (a convention is worth designing when there is more than one case to design it for). D-118's FIRST half is untouched and still current: `pvs.rs` is over the cap, its why is the one that line records, and the honest reduction is still scheduled for WP-1.5 — flips never; this is a deferral ending, not a decision reversing.

D-133: Amends D-117's cut in one place and nowhere else: WP-1.2 splits into **WP-1.2a** opening corpus extraction and fixture curation, then **WP-1.2b** minimal pistol-arena. Order is unchanged, everything from WP-1.3 onward keeps its number, and D-117's argument for why the arena sits second is untouched. The reason for the cut is what the two halves are made of: 1.2a is data work — choosing paired openings, balancing them, and pinning them into the sha-indexed fixture form a runner reads — with no runner in it, and 1.2b is a match runner, an SPRT, a dedupe and a compute ledger with no judgement about positions in it. A single package holding both lands neither under review, because a reviewer attacking the corpus and a reviewer attacking the harness are reading for different failures and the one report would carry both badly. The split also puts the corpus where the WPs after it can see it: WP-1.3's calibration experiments are paired-opening SPRTs (D-117), so the openings are their input, and a corpus that arrives inside the runner's own package is a corpus nobody reviewed on its own terms. No renumbering, deliberately: D-117's numbers are cited from ROADMAP.md, from work-package prompts and from this file, and a renumber to close a letter gap would invalidate every one of those citations to buy nothing — flips per WP, as D-117 says: a cut that moves is an amendment, never a silent reorder.

D-134: Amends what D-126 claims about coverage, on a REVIEW-impl finding with its reproducer. D-126 says D-79's premise "keeps a check rather than losing one", which is true in KIND and not in coverage, and the difference is large enough that a reader who took the sentence at face value would over-rate the suite. Before: `record`'s `REFERENCE_PAIR_ORDER_DISAGREES` compared the two orderings of every pair at the root of EVERY reference run — 31 fixtures, three depths, two radii, both tiers, on every commit and every gate. After: `PairOrder::BothOrderings` has two callers, five distinct fixtures between them, radius 1 only, two turns deep. D-126 states the new scope, so the narrowing was derivable, but it never states the old one, and "the check moved" reads as "the check is the same size". What is bought back is a different shape rather than the same shape smaller: the mode comparison compares whole per-turn MAPS instead of catching a disagreement at the node that reached it, which is why the reviewer's own cross-check — the same instrumented walk over 12 272 distinct node positions, plus the deduped root turn set against `generate_turns` at `LEGAL_RADIUS` on two positions where rule 4 actually truncates, 78 072 and 67 288 turns, no turn missing or extra — found the dedupe exact where a value comparison alone would not have proved it. The narrowing is now stated in `tests/common/reference.rs`'s own module doc as well as here — flips if a cheap way to run `BothOrderings` widely appears, which the dedupe itself makes more likely rather than less.

D-135: Amends D-129's example list, and records the tension a REVIEW-impl surfaced in the taxonomy rather than leaving it to be re-derived. Two corrections. D-129 names "coordinate overflow" among the things `assert!` guards; it is not — the guard is `panic!` inside a `checked_*` unwrap under `COORD_OVERFLOW` (D-34, D-44), and the taxonomy says nothing about `panic!`-in-`unwrap_or_else`, which is in fact the workspace's dominant fail-loud device at some two dozen sites. The taxonomy governs the two ASSERTION macros and nothing else; a named `panic!` on a refused `Result` is a third device with its own rule (rule 3), and reading D-129 as covering it would be reading a classification into a line that never made one. The tension, which is real and is not a defect: `pvs.rs` carries the SAME predicate — the phase is a turn boundary — twice, forty lines apart, as a `debug_assert!` at the depth-0 horizon and an `assert!` at the empty-candidate horizon, with the same consequence on violation (a static value returned mid-turn, which is a wrong answer). Under D-129's primary test the first would be an `assert!`; it is a `debug_assert!` on the cost clause alone, because it sits at every leaf while the other sits in a branch that is unreachable for any radius of at least one (D-104) and therefore costs nothing. That is the ruling as written and it is followed as written; what was missing is the sentence saying the two are the same statement priced differently, which is what D-128's `release-checked` profile exists to collapse — flips if the cost clause is ever measured to be worth less than the confusion, which is a rule-5 bench and a new line here.

D-136: `corpus-extract` is a SECOND BINARY in pistol-cli, not a `pistol` subcommand and not pistol-arena. This amends CLAUDE.md's crate map, which lists pistol-cli's binaries by enumeration — line-protocol engine, perft, bench, selftest — and this is not among them; the amendment is stated here rather than read into the map, because a map that licenses anything licenses nothing. Not a `pistol` subcommand: that binary builds an engine from a config on every path and this one builds none, so the two would share a program and nothing else. The determinism-gate argument for the split is NOT the reason and is recorded as rejected — `tools/determinism.sh` runs named commands and a subcommand that constructs no engine cannot dilute D-7's one-engine-construction path; the real reason is that a one-shot curation tool has no business linked into the program that ships. Not pistol-arena, whose map line does name "paired openings" and is therefore a genuine claim on this work: D-133 cut WP-1.2a to have no runner in it, and the deciding practical fact is that the extractor needs SHA-256 at run time, which pistol-cli already has and pistol-arena does not — putting it there would grow the workspace's third copy of a hash — flips when pistol-arena exists and wants the extractor beside the runner that reads its output, which is a move of one binary and no rules.

D-137: The twelve symmetries of the hex lattice land in pistol-core NOW, as `symmetry.rs`, and the opening corpus deduplicates by `canonical_form` rather than by position identity. The slot was already reserved verbatim in pistol-core's own `lib.rs` for Stage 5's opening book, so this is Stage-5 work pulled forward rather than scope invented, and it is additive: no pinned constant, no perft count and no existing fixture sha moves. It goes in pistol-core because it is lattice geometry and geometry lives there (CLAUDE.md rule 2) — doing it in the extractor would have been the rule-2 breach the convenience tempted. The measurement that forced it, over the RATED GAMES AT OR ABOVE THE FLOOR AND BEFORE THE MISMATCH CEILING (4380 games — the pool named so the numbers can be reproduced without guessing, since D-142's "eligible" is a narrower set): at K=3 that pool holds 2673 distinct positions but only 1934 symmetry classes (27.6% duplicates), at K=4 3681 and 3289 (10.6%), and in a 200-entry capped set 16 of 200 entries were the mirror image of another entry. CLAUDE.md rule 6 counts distinct games with identical games deduped, and an arena deduplicating by move list provably cannot see these, so the reported distinct-n would have been wrong. The counter-argument is recorded because it is true and it bounds the size of the defect rather than removing it: D-7's final tie-break is lexicographic by `(q, r)` and so is NOT symmetry-invariant, which means two mirrored openings often do not produce mirrored games — they are strongly correlated samples, not identical ones. Translation is deliberately excluded from the group (it would collapse K=3's 1934 to 1749): rule 3 anchors every position at the origin, so a translated position is not a position this game reaches — flips if a fixture ever needs shape equivalence rather than position equivalence, which the opening book might.

D-138: An opening is K = 4 TURNS, seven stones, both sides having had two turns. The first design said three turns and gave three reasons, two of which were wrong and are recorded as withdrawn so nobody re-derives them: (a) "K=4 shrinks the distinct pool" is backwards — prefixes are nested, so distinct-position supply is monotone non-decreasing in K, and the measurement — over the same rated-and-floored pool D-137 names, 4380 games — is 535 positions at K=2, 2673 at K=3, 3681 at K=4, with symmetry classes 212 / 1934 / 3289; on the narrower set the ceiling leaves, K=4 is 1739 distinct and 1591 canonical, which is the fixture; (b) "far enough from the origin that the radius-8 region is open" distinguishes nothing, since a radius-8 ball holds 217 cells and the region is wide open after the first stone. What survives is that K=3 hands P2 a position in which P1 has moved twice and P2 once, while K=4 gives each side two turns, and that K=4 has 70% more symmetry-distinct openings at a quarter of K=3's duplicate rate. The honest cost is recorded too: a longer prefix is more committed and therefore more lopsided — of the canonical classes with at least ten corpus games, 33% fall outside a 0.35-0.65 first-player win rate at K=3 and 43% at K=4. K is the wrong instrument for balance, which is what D-145 is for — flips if WP-1.2b measures transposition between shallow openings, which would argue for going deeper still.

D-139: The corpus reader accepts the SCHEMA'S grammar, not JSON's, and every deviation is a named refusal. `serde_json` was never an option — `crates/pistol-cli/tests/workspace_shape_tests.rs` pins every crate in this workspace to `pistol-*`, `serde`, `toml`, `serde_path_to_error` — but the choice that mattered was between a general hand-rolled JSON value parser and a narrow one, and the first design chose the general one on the grounds that ad-hoc parsing turns malformed input into wrong answers. The conclusion was right and the inference inverted: a general parser's risk lives in the features this corpus never uses — `\uXXXX` and surrogate pairs, exponents and fractions, nested containers — which is surface no test here would exercise and no corpus would reveal, whereas a reader accepting only the schema's shape CANNOT silently mis-read, because anything else is a refusal. So no escapes, no floats, no exponents, no nesting beyond the schema's, a `\r` refused rather than trimmed, a blank line refused, and `source` pinned to `human`; `SCHEMA.md` permits `elo` to be absent under `--no-meta` and this tool requires it, which is a stated narrowing rather than an assumption. It also keeps the file under rule 9's cap, which the general parser would not have — flips if a future corpus legitimately needs a JSON feature, at which point the reader grows that feature by name.

D-140: A corpus move's element zero is `q` and element one is `r`, pinned by a parser test on a move whose components differ. This is a rule-3 line rather than a triviality, because NOTHING DOWNSTREAM CAN CATCH THE SWAP: q<->r is one of D-137's twelve lattice automorphisms, verified to preserve hex distance and to permute the three axes onto themselves, so a reader with the mapping backwards produces a perfectly legal, perfectly self-consistent, REFLECTED corpus — every game replays, every winner agrees, zero exclusions, and the replay oracle reports success. The oracle's blindness is named in the module doc beside the test, because the oracle is otherwise this work package's strongest instrument and a reader could reasonably assume it covers this — flips never; it is a fact about the geometry.

D-141: The recorded-order cross-check counts two things `make_turn` cannot see, and each has a fixture that makes its count exactly one. A pair is legal iff SOME ordering of its placements is (D-6, D-51), so the turn-level oracle is the right eligibility filter and is structurally blind to what the record's own order did: **order-rescued**, where the recorded first stone is outside the legal region and the pair plays reversed, and **stone-after-win**, where the recorded first stone already completes a line so the record's second stone follows a decided game while the same pair played the other way round is an ordinary turn. Both measure zero on the real corpus, and that is only worth stating because the two fixtures show the counters moving: a REVIEW-design finding, verified with its own reproducer, was that an implementation hard-coding both counts to zero would pass every other test, pass the real run and print the headline — an unfalsifiable measurement recorded in an ADR being worse than no measurement. The check folds into the single replay pass as a `place` / classify / `undo` probe rather than a second full replay, which also removes the question of what a second replay does after it diverges. Exhaustiveness is proved rather than assumed, and this line states the mechanism the code actually uses rather than the one an earlier draft described: the two classes are read from what the probe DID — a refusal with `OutsideLegalRegion` is order-rescued, and a SUCCESSFUL `PlyOutcome::Win` on a turn that has a second stone is stone-after-win. `GameDecided` is not the stone-after-win signal and is in fact unreachable, because the loop returns `PostWinContinuation` at the top of every iteration before any probe; it panics, as do `OccupiedCell` and `FirstStoneNotAtOrigin`. The statement order is load-bearing — the probe's verdict is matched only after `make_turn` has returned `Ok` — and `replay.rs`'s module doc now says so, because hoisting that match for readability would turn an ordinary named exclusion into a panic — flips never.

D-142: Opening eligibility is a TWO-SIDED rating band: `|elo_p1 - elo_p2| <= 100`, then `min(elo) >= M` where M is the lower median of `min(elo)` over the games meeting every other clause (element `(n-1)/2` of the ascending sort — an integer, no averaging, no rounding rule). The floor alone, which the work package specified, was measured INERT and that finding is the reason the ceiling exists: with the priority rule and a 200-entry cap the emitted set was byte-identical with and without it, because the 200th pick had min-elo 1310 against a median of 996. The ceiling is derived from the corpus and the criterion was fixed before the yield was read: the higher-rated player scores .532, .558 and .609 in the gap buckets below 100 and then .675, .747, .860 and .941 above it, so 100 is the largest round gap at which every bucket keeps the favourite under .61 — below it an opening is a contest both sides contributed to, above it one side was outclassed and half the opening is that player's mistake. The comparison is INCLUSIVE (`gap <= 100`) while the buckets that derived it are half-open, so the 30 candidate games at a gap of exactly 100 sit in the .675 bucket and are admitted; the discrepancy is named rather than left for a reader to find, and it is 30 games in 3908. Consequences, not reasons: 3908 candidates, M = 997, 1956 eligible games. What the band does NOT buy is balance, and the ADR says so — the first-player win rate is 0.5022 overall, 0.5021 above the median and 0.5023 below it — flips if a corpus arrives whose ratings are on another scale, since 100 is an Elo distance and not a quantile.

D-143: The openings fixture has NO CAP and is emitted in `game_hash` order. The work package specified a cap of 200 by a priority of higher min-elo then lower hash; both REVIEW-design agents found the number underived, and the measurement behind dropping it is that in a deterministic instrument mode the book is the only source of game diversity, so 200 openings is 400 games and no more — about 40 normalized Elo of resolution, where the research report's SPRT bounds want thousands. A cap that cannot be relaxed downstream is a ceiling on Stage 1's whole ability to accept or reject its own work, and there is no size argument for it: the full pool is 1591 openings and about 140 kB, some 1.4% of rule 7's ceiling. The priority rule survives with its real job — choosing which game REPRESENTS a canonical class — and the emission order is the hash instead, because with no cap a runner takes a prefix, and a prefix of a rating-sorted pool is the extreme tail rather than a sample (the 200 openings the old rule would have emitted came from a 239-game slice of 8698). WP-1.2b pre-registers its own n in its own validated config, where CLAUDE.md rule 1 already governs it — flips if a fixture consumer turns out to need a pre-committed subset, which is a second file and not a truncation of this one.

D-144: SHA-256 moves from pistol-cli's test tree into the crate's library as a PUBLIC module. WP-1.2a turned the digest from something a test checks into something a program computes — `corpus-extract` hashes the corpus it read and the payload it wrote — and a digest a binary needs at run time is library code. It is `pub` rather than `pub(crate)` against a REVIEW-design recommendation, and the reason is recorded because the recommendation's premise is right in general: this crate's public surface is the contract the API layer will adapt (rule 11) and a hash is no part of it. But an integration test is a separate crate and cannot see `pub(crate)`, and `tests/tactical_v0_tests.rs` pins the tactical fixture with this digest, so hiding it would have left that test needing a second copy INSIDE pistol-cli — precisely what promoting the file was meant to stop. The FIPS 180-4 vectors move with the implementation as a `#[cfg(test)]` unit test, so the hash that computes every pin is still itself pinned. D-37 is untouched and does not apply: it makes pistol-core std-only including dev-dependencies, so that crate's test tree keeps its own copy and cannot do otherwise — flips if the workspace ever takes a hashing dependency.

D-145: The openings fixture EMITS the corpus's own outcome evidence per opening — how many corpus games reach it up to a symmetry, and how many of those the first player won — and acts on none of it. ROADMAP's WP-1.2a line and D-133 both name "balance" as this package's charter, and the first design's answer was that paired play makes it moot. That is half right and the wrong half is expensive: playing each opening from both sides cancels colour BIAS exactly, but it does not recover the power lost to a lopsided opening, because under determinism a decided opening yields a fixed 1-1 pair carrying no information — and D-143 has already established that the games cannot be bought back by playing more. The corpus says human openings are not balanced: of the canonical K=4 classes with at least ten games, the first-player rate runs 0.10 to 0.91 and 26 of 61 fall outside 0.35-0.65. Emitting the evidence rather than thresholding on it is deliberate — a threshold is the runner's to pre-register, and the report's literal recipe (filter by |eval| below a balance threshold) would put the engine under test into its own book. The coverage limit is stated in the fixture header rather than implied: of 5941 canonical classes, 885 have two or more games and 61 have ten or more, so most lines read `games 1` and the evidence speaks for part of the pool — flips when an engine strong enough to be trusted as a neutral judge exists, which is a Stage-5 book question.

D-146: A bench position is the prefix at the LARGEST ODD STONE COUNT at or below the band centre and no lower than the centre less the width, strictly fewer than the game's own stones. This is the rule the work package's "15±2 / 35±5, first index entering the band" actually behaves as, spelled the way it behaves: a position must sit at a turn boundary to be a move list at all (D-6) and turn t carries 2t-1 stones, so only odd counts are reachable, and "closest to the centre" always lands at or below it — on the real corpus band 15 selects 15 in all 8698 games and band 35 selects 35, 33 or 31 and never 37 or 39. Shipping a symmetric ± of which half provably never fires would have been shipping a parameter that does nothing. Twelve per band, in `game_hash` order because a content hash cannot be cherry-picked, and NO GAME IN BOTH BANDS: twenty-four games measure twenty-four position shapes where twelve measured twice would measure twelve, at the same cost. A REVIEW-design proposal to stratify the selection by legal-region size was declined — it is a curation choice nobody pre-registered — and the concern it raised is answered instead by reporting each selected position's stone count in the file. Named consumer, which the first design lacked: ROADMAP WP-1.3(c)'s fixed-node runs at two stone counts, D-127 having already measured against two ad-hoc positions — flips if WP-1.3 wants a third band.

D-147: Both fixtures are serialized by a stated discipline, because a digest pinned over an under-specified serialization pins an accident (CLAUDE.md rule 4). Lines end `\n` and the file ends with exactly one; the header identifies the corpus by SHA-256 AND BY NOTHING ELSE — no path, no timestamp, no hostname, no version, no git SHA, so two machines given the same bytes write the same file and a header carrying a path would have made "identical inputs, identical outputs" false between two machines that both did everything right; `# param` lines carry inputs and `# derived` lines carry computed values, so a reader reproducing the file can tell a choice from a measurement; the exclusion list is ordered by game hash, capped, and written `# excluded none` when empty, because a missing section and an empty one must not look alike; and the body begins at the first byte after the newline ending the `# body_sha256` line, which is stated because the payload contains `#` comment lines of its own and "the leading run of comments" would not have been a usable rule — flips never without a new fixture version.

D-148: Each fixture carries a `# body_sha256` over its payload AND is pinned by whole-file digest in the test that reads it. The first design justified the pair by saying they catch different edits, which is wrong and is corrected here: the whole-file digest changes on any byte anywhere and so strictly dominates for edit detection. The body digest earns its place for a different reason — it is IN-BAND, so a consumer holding only the file, which is what pistol-arena will be at load time, can refuse a corrupted fixture without carrying an out-of-band constant from someone else's test tree (rule 3). WP-1.2b is expected to verify it; if it does not, the body digest is dead weight and should go — flips on that.

D-149: The replay result, which is this work package's most valuable output and the reason the extractor exists at all. All 8698 games of the human corpus replay through pistol-core under the full rule set — turn structure, occupancy, origin opening, win detection, rule 4's truncation, and the radius-8 legal region — with ZERO failures in every class: zero illegal turns, zero post-win continuations, zero winner mismatches, zero games left undecided, zero order-rescued turns and zero stones recorded after a winning one. The winner pistol-core computes agrees with the corpus's independently exported `winner` field on all 8698. This is the first independent evidence for D-101, which resolved the radius-8 question by operator ruling against an evidential gap: radius 8 appears nowhere in the corpus's `SCHEMA.md`, `README.md` or `dataset_metadata.json`, and 8698 real platform games now replay inside it without one exception. Rule 4 fires in the wild: 151 games end on a turn's first stone with the second never played. Alongside, the first look at the report's section-F fairness question, WITH ITS CONFOUND NAMED rather than claimed as an answer — first player wins 4368/8698 (0.5022) overall, 2199/4380 above the rating median and 2169/4318 below it, and among evenly matched games (rating gap under 25, n = 1096) 530/1096 (0.4836, ±2.96% at 95%), mildly defender-leaning and not distinguishable from even. A rated human corpus CANNOT answer the game-theoretic question: seat assignment is independent of strength, so the aggregate is about even by construction of the rating pool whatever the game's intrinsic tilt, and the confound is visible in the same data — among the games D-142's ceiling excludes, gap strictly over 100, the higher-rated player scores 3856/4790 (0.8050). (At gap 100 or more, which is the half-open bucket D-142 derives from, it is 3877/4820 (0.8044); the stats block reports the first, because that is the population the ceiling removes.) Section F stays open for engine self-play in WP-1.2b — flips on a corpus that does not replay clean, which is a rules-truth escalation and not a data problem.

D-150: Puzzle mining is DEFERRED to a named second pass, pre-registered here so it is not re-proposed as an oversight. Mining mate-in-n and must-block positions over every position of every corpus game needs fixed-depth sweeps that are unaffordable full-width — WP-1.1's own oracle pays the candidate count squared per turn, which is minutes of release CPU for a third turn on ONE position — so the pass belongs after WP-1.5's threat machinery makes a bounded forcing search cheap, and it reads the same corpus by the same sha. What WP-1.2a ships instead is the two fixtures the arena needs now; the tactical fixture class those puzzles would join is `tactical_v0.txt`'s successor and will pre-register its own threshold below 100%, per that file's own header — flips when WP-1.5 lands and the sweep is affordable.

D-151: `openings_v1.txt` is a FIXTURE under CLAUDE.md rule 7, not a book under rule 8, and the distinction is written down here because it is exactly the kind rule 10 exists for. Rule 8 says nets, books, match logs and bench outputs are never committed; this file is a committed list of opening positions, so the question is fair. What makes it a fixture is what is in it: corpus provenance and nothing else — a position, the game it came from, that game's lower rating, and the corpus's own win counts for its symmetry class. No engine judgement, no eval, no search result, no solved value. A book is a store of the engine's OWN conclusions and is regenerated whenever the engine changes; this is a store of what humans played, is regenerated only when the corpus changes, and is pinned by digest precisely so that it cannot drift (D-147, D-148). It is 140 kB against rule 7's 10 MB ceiling. The corpus it derives from stays uncommitted, which is the rule-8 obligation that does bind here — flips the moment a curation step consults an engine, which D-145 declines to do for its own reasons; a balance-filtered book WOULD be a book.

D-152: Records the WP-1.2a review round, because three of its findings are amendments to lines above rather than defects in code, and a reader of D-136..D-151 should know which sentences were corrected and why. REVIEW-design attacked the four parameters the work package invited attack on and all four moved: K went 3 -> 4, the cap went 200 -> none, the dedupe key went position identity -> canonical form, and the elo rule gained a mismatch ceiling — each recorded in its own line with the measurement that moved it. REVIEW-impl then found that the committed fixtures had been generated BEFORE the ADR citations in their own header prose were renumbered, so the shipped artifacts cited D-144/D-146/D-147 where the source now said D-143/D-145/D-146, and the sha pins certified bytes the build could no longer produce — a rule-4 and rule-7 breach that the whole suite was structurally unable to see, because every header test read the committed bytes and never bytes the tool had just written. That hole is now closed by two tests over produced output, one of which compares the header prose block against the committed one, so an edit to the prose without a regeneration is a red test. The same pass found four curation clauses whose tests asserted a constant against itself — `gap <= ELO_GAP_CEILING` is true whatever the constant holds — and each is now pinned by its consequence instead; the surviving mutations are listed in the session report. RED-TEAM ran some seventy adversarial documents and found every malformed one refused by name at exit 2 and every rules-level failure excluded by name at exit 1, but caught an empty candidate set aborting through an `assert!` at exit 101 and discarding the stats block, which is the escalation output — now a named refusal that prints the measurement first — flips never; this line is history, and the lines it describes are the record.

D-153: The arena's budget section spells all THREE budget kinds, including the `movetime_ms` it refuses, and the refusal is its own named error citing the reason. Leaving the variant out of the schema would have been shorter and would have made `serde` answer "unknown variant, expected one of depth_turns, nodes", which points at the schema and tells an operator nothing about why wall-clock is not admissible here. This is D-22's shape moved up a layer: the enum is closed and complete, and the layer that cannot honour a member refuses it by name rather than by omission. The text cites CLAUDE.md rule 6 (every strength claim comes from an instrument budget) AND docs/decisions.md D-95 (a movetime budget is a floor rather than a ceiling, because the first deepening iteration is not interruptible), because those are two different objections and an operator who worked around the first would still be caught by the second. `arena_refuses_movetime_budget_with_named_error` additionally asserts that the same validator ACCEPTS `depth_turns` and `nodes`, so it cannot pass against a validator that refuses every budget — flips by the ADR that lets a wall-clock run make a strength claim, which is WP-1.4 and Stage 4 at the earliest.

D-154: The verdict is read off the PAIR-level GSPRT and the game-level LLR is demoted to a reported diagnostic. OPERATOR RULING, and it overrides the work package's own pre-registration, which said the v0 verdict would be game-level; the ruling is recorded here rather than in the code because changing a pre-registration is an operator act. Both REVIEW-design agents attacked the pre-registered choice independently and the design's defence of it did not survive. What the design asserted — that the game-level test is "roughly a factor of two anti-conservative" — is wrong, and wrong in DIRECTION as often as in magnitude. The derivation, since an asserted magnitude is what got this wrong the first time: write the LLR as an evidence term minus a drift term; the sample mean is identical at both units, so the two differ only through sigma, and `var_pair <= var_game` always (with equality only when no pair is 1-1). The factor of two is therefore a strict upper bound attained only at perfect within-pair correlation, and once 1-1 pairs are common the game-level test is CONSERVATIVE. Measured on a constructed sample of 200 pairs of which 150 are 1-1: `llr_game` 1.1625 against `llr_pair` 1.8535, the game-level statistic understating the evidence by 37%. Two deterministic engines at a fixed budget produce exactly that regime, so the direction an operator would have guessed is the wrong one. The rejected alternatives are recorded because this ruling is re-openable: (a) KEEP THE GAME-LEVEL VERDICT as pre-registered and report the disagreement factor `2*sqrt(var_pair/var_game)` beside it, which is honest and costs nothing but ships a verdict known to be wrong in a direction the run itself determines; (b) REQUIRE BOTH UNITS TO AGREE, verdict `inconclusive_split` otherwise, which is strictly more conservative and spends real games on the finite opening pool to buy certainty the SPRT already prices. Reporting both without a binding rule was rejected outright on a reviewer's argument that `nElo_pair >= nElo_game` unconditionally, so an operator can predict which number flatters a result before running it, which is a garden of forking paths inside the tool whose whole job is to stop one — flips at Stage 5's pentanomial manager, which changes the scheduling around this statistic and not the statistic.

D-155: The estimator is the closed-form Gaussian GSPRT in normalized Elo, `LLR = n * ((t1 - t0) * (mu - 1/2)/sqrt(var) - (t1^2 - t0^2)/2)` with `t_k = elo_k * ln(10)/800`, and not the exact multinomial GSPRT. The deciding reason is this work package's own requirement that the math be pinned by a table of HAND-COMPUTED values: the exact GSPRT needs a constrained maximum-likelihood tilt found by a one-dimensional root search, which nobody computes by hand, and a reference table that can only be produced by the implementation under test pins nothing. The scale factor is `800/ln(10)` and not `1600/ln(10)`: from `mu = 1/(1+10^(-Elo/400))`, `mu - 1/2 ~= Elo*ln(10)/1600`, and normalized Elo is defined to equal logistic Elo at `sigma = 1/2`, where `t = (mu-1/2)/sigma = 2(mu-1/2) = Elo*ln(10)/800`. Both reviewers re-derived it independently and it is also consistent with the research report's `640000/nElo^2` rule of thumb, which `1600/ln(10)` misses by a factor of four. The pair unit uses `t_k * sqrt(2)`, which is not a fudge: normalized Elo is defined on the per-GAME scale, so a pair's hypotheses must be written in per-game sigma, `sigma_per_game = sqrt(2 * var_pair)`, and substituting reproduces the same expression with the hypotheses scaled. `the_pair_unit_answers_the_same_hypothesis_as_the_game_unit` pins that the two agree exactly on an independent-limit sample, which is the property the scaling exists to give and which a missing `sqrt(2)` would break. The estimator is a PROFILE likelihood ratio, sigma being re-estimated at every prefix, so the Wald bounds are approximate exactly as they are in Fishtest, and the module says so beside them. Arithmetic is bit-reproducible by correct rounding and a fixed expression order rather than by exactness: no `mul_add`, no reordered summation, variance in the raw-moment form the reference table pins, `ln(10)` a compile-time constant, and the only libm calls in a whole verdict are the two Wald bounds — so a verdict could differ across libm implementations only when an LLR lands on a bound to the last bit — flips at Stage 5, where an exact GSPRT can be cross-checked numerically against an external implementation instead of by hand.

D-156: There is NO regularization of zero counts. A sample with zero variance has no likelihood ratio, and the verdict token says `inconclusive_degenerate` rather than carrying a number. OPERATOR RULING. The design proposed Fishtest's pseudo-count of 1e-3 and argued it was part of the estimator's definition rather than a tunable; a reviewer refuted that with a reproducer on this work package's own smoke shape. At `n = 8`, `w = 8`, `elo1 = 4`, the LLR is 1.163 at a pseudo-count of 1e-2 and does not cross, and 3.683 at 1e-3 and crosses to `h1`, scaling as the pseudo-count to the power of minus a half. A constant that flips a verdict is a tunable whatever an ADR calls it, and a tunable lives in exactly one schema place (CLAUDE.md rule 1). The Gaussian likelihood ratio is meaningless in that regime anyway: the sample mean sits some forty sample-sigmas from BOTH hypotheses and the statistic still reports evidence. The rejected alternatives, since this is re-openable: (a) MAKE IT AN EXPLICIT `[sprt]` KEY with no code-side default, which satisfies rule 1 and hands an operator a knob whose statistical meaning is nil; (b) REFUSE PLUS AN EXPLICIT `min_pairs_before_stop`, also pre-registered, which additionally keeps the sequential rule out of the small-sample regime. (b)'s second half turned out to be unnecessary rather than wrong: a degenerate sample cannot cross a boundary either, so the refusal is already the stop guard and the spurious early crossing a reviewer demonstrated cannot occur. The stated cost of the ruling is accepted: an engine that wins every game reports `inconclusive_degenerate` forever, and the report's `8-0-0` and its pentanomial are what an operator reads instead — flips if a run ever legitimately needs to conclude from a shutout, which would be an argument for (a) with the constant pinned by its own reference-table row.

D-157: `run.openings_take` is the run's only size knob and the game cap is derived as twice it; `capped_fraction` is REPORTED and not thresholded on. Two decisions in one line because both are about not stating a number twice. The first: every opening is exactly one pair, so a separate `game_cap` was inert config wherever it was not simply `2 * openings_take`, and its evenness rule then meant two different things in two places — a reviewer found the design's own stopping rule violating the parity rule its own config validation enforced. The second is an OPERATOR RULING, and it is the one place this work package leaves a known lever unguarded. `turn_cap` is pinned as an evaluation horizon and never a game rule, but capped games are not inert in the statistic: normalized Elo is variance-normalized, a mass point at a half shrinks sigma, and for a FIXED decisive record adding capped games ACCELERATES the LLR toward H1 — measured, a 100-80 record scores 0.2198 with no capped games, 0.6329 with 1800, and about 1.111 at the maximum. The design's first draft stated this cost BACKWARDS, claiming capped games shrink the effective sample, and that sentence is withdrawn here so nobody cites it. The rejected alternative is a pre-registered `capped_fraction_ceiling` in `[sprt]` yielding a verdict of `inconclusive_horizon` above it, which is what a reviewer proposed and what rule 5's no-post-hoc-thresholds argument favours; the ruling is to report the fraction and let an operator judge the run, which trades that guard for less schema. What makes the unguarded version survivable is that an all-capped run is degenerate under D-156 and so cannot report `h0` or `h1` at all — flips the first time a real experiment's verdict turns on its capped fraction, which the reported number will make visible.

D-158: A forfeit is a game outcome AND it invalidates the run's verdict token, not merely its exit code. The offender loses the game, and the report carries the offending party, the reason, the turn and the engine's verbatim refusal — the work package pre-registered "a named reason in the report", and aborting the run instead would write no report at all. But a forfeit in a pistol-versus-pistol match means one of the two configurations is broken, and a reviewer's reproducer is decisive: point engine B at a stub that always plays an illegal turn, and every game forfeits, A scores 8-0, the LLR crosses, and `grep '^verdict ' report.txt` answers `h1`. A count on a neighbouring line does not fix that, and neither does an exit code, which is gone by the time a report is pasted into an ADR. So the token itself reads `invalid_forfeit`, the would-be conclusion moves to a separate `verdict_if_clean` line — hiding it would be the silent skip rule 3 forbids — and the process additionally exits non-zero because a script reads that and a human reads the file. `result` and `end` stay two fields for the same reason: a forfeit is a LOSS, so the winner is known, and collapsing them into `result forfeit` would throw the winner away and leave a reason with no party attached to it — flips if an external opponent is ever admitted (Stage 5+), where a forfeit is an ordinary match event rather than evidence of a bug in one's own engine.

D-159: Silence abandons the RUN and is never adjudicated; a child that EXITED WITH A CODE forfeits, and a child killed by a SIGNAL or a spawn that failed abandons the run like silence. The first half is the determinism law applied to the referee: a timeout that forfeited a game would make the verdict a function of how fast the machine is, so the same two engines over the same openings would report differently on a loaded box and an idle one — inside the instrument every strength claim comes from (CLAUDE.md rule 4). The second half is a reviewer's finding against the design's first draft, which forfeited on any closed pipe. The counter-example is concrete: run at eight workers on a memory-tight box and the OOM killer takes children, which arrives at the arena as an EOF indistinguishable from `exit(1)` — so the design's stated distinction, that a closed pipe is "a deterministic answer to a deterministic input", was an assumption about the ENVIRONMENT rather than a property of the protocol. `ExitStatus::code()` tells them apart on Unix, returning `Some` for a self-chosen exit and `None` for a signal, and the exit code or the signal is recorded either way because `engine_exited` with no status is undiagnosable. `hang_timeout_ms` is explicit config with no default; it satisfies rule 1 because it has a schema place, and it satisfies rule 4 because it can never reach a reported number. There is no wall-clock-free liveness signal available to replace it: D-2 pins the verb set with no stop and no heartbeat, and a truly hung engine emits nothing at all — flips never while instrument mode is the source of strength claims.

D-160: A run that is abandoned still writes a report, whose FIRST-LINE TOKEN is `arena_report_aborted` rather than `arena_report`, and which carries no `verdict` line and no LLR. The design's first draft wrote nothing, which both reviewers attacked from the same direction: a hang on game 1500 of 1591 would discard every completed game, and D-159's actual requirement is only that no REPORTED NUMBER depend on wall-clock — not that the evidence be destroyed. A different first-line token rather than a flag on the same one, because a consumer that greps for `verdict` must not be able to find one on a run that did not produce one, and because the games in an aborted report are a diagnostic rather than a sample: WHICH games finished before the abort depends on timing, and the file says so in a comment line above them. `arena_aborts_run_when_engine_hangs` asserts the kind token, the absence of any `verdict` line, and the presence of a named `aborted Hung` line — which is a stronger assertion than "no file exists", and one that cannot pass vacuously — flips never.

D-161: The report splits at a `# timing` marker into a verdict block that is worker-invariant and byte-comparable and a timing block that is machine- and schedule-dependent, and the invariance is claimed only for runs that COMPLETE. The claim is stated with that qualification because it is false without it: a watchdog sized against one worker can fire at eight, and then two worker counts produce a report and nothing rather than two equal reports. Engine `time_ms` cannot be invariant — two games contending for a core change it — and neither can the count of in-flight games abandoned at the stop, so they are named, segregated and excluded by construction rather than wished away. This is what `tools/determinism.sh` already does with `nps` and `time` (D-7). One consequence was found by the test rather than by the design: the arena config's own digest is NOT invariant either, because `n_workers` lives in that document, so the verdict block carries an `experiment_sha256` over the experiment-defining values only — the openings body digest, the take, the turn cap, the budget, the SPRT bounds and each engine's binary and config digests — while the document's own digest is provenance and sits in the timing block. Identifying engines by DIGEST rather than by path is the same rule D-147 applied to the corpus: `target/release/pistol` is a different program after every build, and a report that named it by path would identify two experiments identically — flips never.
