D-162: The arena refuses, at the handshake and before a single game, an engine that reports a protocol version it does not speak or a mode other than `instrument`. The mode check is the load-bearing one: every strength claim comes from an instrument mode (CLAUDE.md rule 6) and instrument mode is where `threads = 1` is enforced (D-7), but a play-mode engine given a depth budget is a perfectly legal request that nothing else in the stack questions — the engine's own `Budget::check_supported` refuses only a wall-clock budget — so this is the only place the rule can be enforced at all. The version check exists because the two sides may be DISTINCT BUILDS, which is the point of naming a binary per configuration, so the arena may not assume the program it spawned speaks the protocol it was compiled against. Both are covered by a stub behaviour rather than by inspection, because a version comparison against an in-tree binary always passes and deleting it would turn nothing red — flips when a deterministic multi-threaded scheduling mode exists (Stage 4), which would be a third mode token and its own line here.

D-163: The distinct-game key is the canonical form of the ORDERED TURN SEQUENCE under the twelve lattice symmetries, and it lands in pistol-core as `canonical_sequence` beside `canonical_form` rather than being composed in the arena. It is not `canonical_form`, and the design's first draft said it was: that function takes a stone MULTISET, sorts the image, and documents that "the order they were played in is not part of the identity this module is about" — so keying a game on it would dedupe by final POSITION and merge two different games that reached the same stones, understating distinct-n, which is the opposite of the error symmetry folding exists to prevent. A reviewer found this by reading the function rather than by running anything, and `two_games_reaching_the_same_stones_are_two_distinct_games` pins it with two games that differ only in the order the first player played its two pairs — the fixture's first draft got even that wrong by redistributing stones ACROSS turns, which changes their colour and makes the positions differ too, so the test would have proved nothing. It lives in pistol-core because it is lattice geometry and geometry lives there (rule 2); doing it in the arena would have been the convenient rule-2 breach. A transformed pair is re-canonicalized to D-5's `(q, r)` order, because a symmetry does not preserve that order and a key that skipped the step would not be symmetry-invariant at all — `a_transformed_pair_is_returned_in_canonical_order` additionally asserts that some symmetry in its fixture actually reorders a pair, so it cannot pass on a fixture the group happens to leave alone. The limitation is stated rather than implied: the key has no false positives and it does have false NEGATIVES, because D-7's final tie-break is lexicographic and therefore not symmetry-invariant, so two mirrored openings usually do not produce mirrored games (D-137 recorded the same thing). `distinct_n` is therefore an over-count and a bound rather than a census — flips never.

D-164: Every game gets FRESH subprocesses; a channel is never reused across games. Reuse plus `newgame` would be faster and D-7's gate already certifies that `newgame` clears everything, but under N workers the assignment of games to processes changes with N, so any residue `newgame` failed to clear would make the report depend on the worker count — the one thing the scheduler must guarantee it does not (D-161). A process spawn is microseconds against a search. There is a second reason the design did not name and a reviewer did: the claim that a self-match's two games are identical move for move rests on both first-seat processes receiving byte-identical command sequences from a fresh start, and the in-game transposition table persists across turns — flips if process spawn is ever measured as a real fraction of a run (rule 5), at which point the fix is a worker-invariant assignment and not naked reuse.

D-165: The sequential stop is evaluated ONLY at pair boundaries, and `k` is the SMALLEST pair count whose sample crosses, recomputed over the whole finished prefix rather than taken as the first crossing a worker happened to notice. Both halves are needed and both were reviewer findings. Odd `k` splits a pair — one seat's game in and the other's out — and the truncation point is correlated with the outcome of the last included game, since a crossing is likeliest immediately after a decisive one, which is optional-stopping bias applied to the one game whose seat is unmatched; it also destroys the pentanomial the verdict now depends on (D-154). Smallest-crossing rather than first-noticed is what makes `k` a function of the game results alone and therefore independent of the order games finished in, which is what the worker-invariance claim rests on. Games in flight past `k` are killed and discarded; they never contributed to the report, so discarding them cannot bias it, and their count is schedule-dependent and lives in the timing block — flips never.

D-166: `arena-stub-engine` is a second binary in pistol-arena, and this amends CLAUDE.md's crate map the way D-136 amended it for `corpus-extract`. The map's pistol-arena line names paired openings, SPRT, Elo, distinct-game dedupe and per-side compute accounting, and a deliberately misbehaving ENGINE is none of those, so the amendment is stated here rather than read into the map. It exists because the forfeit, garbage, bad-bestmove, exit, hang, wrong-protocol and play-mode paths are otherwise unreachable by any test, and a referee nobody has watched refuse is not a referee. Its protocol conformance is the engine's own code — it implements the `Engine` trait with a one-line search and serves it through the real `pistol_cli::Session`, so only the named deviation is its own. A bin rather than an example because `CARGO_BIN_EXE_<name>` exists for bins only, and a test that guessed at `target/<profile>/examples/...` would break on a profile change. Two guards against it being mistaken for an engine: it refuses to start without an explicit `behave` line in its config, so it can never default to looking like a very weak engine, and it announces itself on stderr. Its behaviour comes from that config file rather than from an environment variable so that two tests running at once cannot change each other's engine. Its search is deliberately NOT `generate_turns`, which enumerates the radius-8 region pairwise and is minutes per move at seven stones; it grows the mover's own cluster instead, which is affordable AND makes games end in wins, where taking the lexicographically smallest legal cells would have produced nothing but capped games and left the win path untested — flips if cargo ever hands tests a resolved path to an example, which would make D-25's precedent apply.

D-167: pistol-arena depends on pistol-cli, and `pistol_arena_manifest_names_only_core_engine_and_cli` pins that it depends on nothing else in this workspace. The dependency is on the crate that owns the LINE PROTOCOL's one spelling (D-5) — the verbs, the `info`/`bestmove`/`error` prefixes, the `totals` marker, the budget words, and the SHA-256 D-144 already made public for exactly this kind of run-time use. A second spelling of those tokens inside the arena would be a second protocol, and the two would drift silently. It is not a rule-11 breach: pistol-cli is not a transport, it is the contract, and the arena is a client of it. The pin is a separate finding: `workspace_shape_tests.rs` already admitted any `pistol-*` dependency by prefix, so without a test of its own the arena could grow a pistol-search or pistol-eval dependency and stay green — the same reach past the seam that `pistol_cli_manifest_names_only_core_and_engine` exists to stop for the CLI — flips if pistol-api needs the same tokens, at which point the protocol vocabulary moves to pistol-engine and both crates adapt.

D-168: The config gate learns a third document kind. `configs/` now holds engine configs, eval weight tables and arena configs, told apart by file name — `*_weights.toml`, `arena_*.toml`, everything else — each going to its own validator, because a document checked against another schema is rejected for every key it does not have (D-64's argument, now with three schemas). The arena's validator is an EXAMPLE rather than a subcommand of `arena`, on D-25's precedent: config checking is a tools-side gate and the binary's surface should not grow a general maintenance command to hold it. In default mode a missing arena config is a gate failure like a missing weight table, because `tools/arena_smoke.sh` runs a committed one — flips never.

D-169: `tools/arena_smoke.sh` is CI gate 11, and it is a SELF-MATCH because that is what makes it assertable. Two identical deterministic engines play the same game whichever seat they sit in, so the whole expected answer is knowable before the run: n is twice the openings, distinct-n is exactly half of n, every pair scores 1-1, the pentanomial's middle bucket holds every pair, and the verdict is `inconclusive_degenerate` — which is the CORRECT answer for two identical configurations and not a failure. A gate whose expected output is "something plausible" is not a gate, so each of those is asserted exactly rather than as a "near-total dedupe" nobody can falsify. It reads the numbers it asserts against out of the config rather than restating them, so it cannot pass after somebody edits the document. It also runs the arena three times: twice at the config's worker count to cover the arena's OWN determinism, which nothing else in this suite covers and which matters because the arena is the instrument every strength claim comes from, and once at one worker to cover D-161's worker-invariance claim — with a positive check that each run recorded its own worker count, so the comparison cannot pass against a report that simply omits the field. Pre-registered cost (rule 5): three runs at `depth_turns 1` and candidate radius 1 over four openings, 24 games and about 480 searches; measured at 3.2 s wall on the development machine including the release build being already warm. The cost grows with `turn_cap` because the candidate set grows with the stone count, so a change to that key is a change to this gate's runtime — flips if the gate's runtime ever crowds out a correctness gate, at which point the openings count is the knob.

D-170: Amends D-165's letter in one clause and nothing else. That line says games in flight past the stop point `k` are "killed and discarded"; they are not killed. The stop is checked before a worker DISPATCHES a game, so a game already running when the bound is crossed is played to completion and then dropped by the truncation. Correctness is untouched — the record never reaches the report, which is what D-165's bias argument actually needs — but the wall-clock cost is real at a worker count above one, and a reader who took the word "killed" at face value would mis-estimate what a stopped run costs. The clause should read: games in flight past `k` are PLAYED OUT and discarded. The alternative, actually killing them, needs a per-game cancellation signal the `Engine` seam deliberately does not have (D-2 pins the verb set with no stop), so it is a Stage-4 question and not a wording fix — flips when a stop verb exists, which Lazy SMP brings.

D-171: Records the WP-1.2b review round, because two of its findings were defects that no gate could see and two more were ADR sentences the code did not honour. REVIEW-impl, against a named revision, in a separate worktree.

**Blocker 1, and the worst defect in the work package.** A closed pipe and an exited process are two events. The reader thread ends at EOF on the child's stdout, which a child can produce while continuing to run; the reaper then called `Child::wait` with no bound, in a place the watchdog cannot reach because control has already left the receive. So an engine that closed its output and kept running hung the arena forever with NO report written — defeating the liveness device D-159 promises and the evidence-keeping D-160 promises, and hanging CI gate 11 rather than failing it. Reproduced with a nine-line shell engine that handshakes and then closes stdout. Fixed: the reap is bounded by the run's own `hang_timeout_ms`, after which the child is killed and classified as a signal death, which routes it to abandon-the-run — a child that stops answering and will not die is machine-dependent in exactly the way a timeout is, and must not adjudicate a game. Pinned by `arena_abandons_a_run_when_an_engine_closes_its_pipe_and_keeps_running`, which asserts a wall-clock bound as well as the report's kind, because an unbounded wait fails no other assertion.

**Blocker 2.** `verdict_if_clean` filtered individual games out of a flat slice. The pentanomial is built from consecutive pairs, so after the first forfeit every pair straddled two different openings and the trailing game vanished unmentioned — a sample nobody computed, printed on the one line that exists to keep a forfeited run honest, and by construction able to read `h1`. That is D-158's own failure mode moved down one line. Fixed by dropping whole pairs (`score::pairs_without_forfeits`), and the count of dropped pairs is now reported, because a conclusion drawn from a smaller sample than the run played is not the same conclusion.

**Two ADR sentences the code did not honour, both now true rather than amended.** D-159 promised the signal would be recorded and the code emitted a constant string for every signal death, which cannot tell an OOM kill from a crash — the signal number is now in the message. Two module docs claimed the handshake `id` lines were copied into the report; they were gathered and discarded, and no `engine_id` line was ever emitted, so the run's instrument was missing the candidate radius and the table size that make it re-runnable (rule 6). The engines are now handshaken once before the run to gather them, which additionally moves a mode or protocol refusal from "abandon a started run" to "refuse before any work" — exit 2 and no report, which is what the binary's own documented exit semantics always said.

**The coverage gap that mattered most.** Every end-to-end test was a self-match, where both games of a pair are the same game and every pair therefore scores alike, so no sample could ever cross a bound: the sequential stop, its pair-boundary rule, its truncation and the discarded count had no test at any level, and both worker-invariance checks would have passed unchanged with the whole stop block deleted. Closed by giving the stub a mirror-image mode — same code, largest cells instead of smallest — so two well-behaved deterministic engines win different openings and produce real pair-to-pair variation (measured over 80 openings: buckets 9 / 0 / 49 / 2 / 20, nothing degenerate, zero duplicate games). `stop_tests.rs` now runs a crossing sample at one worker and at four and compares the truncation point and the verdict block.

**Four tests that were weaker than they read.** The pair-unit equivalence test used a sample with mean exactly one half, where the evidence term vanishes on both sides, so only the drift term was ever compared — the property the `sqrt(2)` exists to give was untested; it now uses an asymmetric record (200 games at 120-80 against 100 pairs at 16/0/48/0/36, both giving 0.4567584686550011, difference exactly zero) and asserts that an unscaled pair value would visibly differ. The normalized-Elo test compared an expression against itself; it now asserts 800/ln(10) and a point estimate by value. And a stated intermediate in the reference table was wrong at the sixth significant figure — the assertions were right, but D-155's whole argument is that a reviewer recomputes the table from the stated intermediates, and that one did not reproduce. Recorded because a hand-computed table with an unreproducible intermediate is the failure mode D-155 exists to avoid, found in the very table it argues for.

**Also fixed, each cheap and each a real hole.** The stop rescored every prefix from scratch after every completed game, which is the pair count squared per game and the run's length cubed overall — some 8e9 record visits at the 1591-opening book this arena exists to play; it is now accumulated. `verdict_block` split on an unanchored substring, so an engine's verbatim refusal containing `# timing` could truncate the block the worker-invariance test compares — it is anchored at a line start. An info-line check lacked its trailing space, so a line beginning `information:` was swallowed as a report instead of forfeiting as a protocol error (rule 3). `score::verdict` carried an `exhausted` parameter whose two branches returned the same value — a parameter no test could have caught going wrong. `Channel::try_receive` and `ArenaError::has_partial_run` were dead: the second is worse than unused, because it encoded a policy about which failures keep their evidence that nothing enforced, while the actual rule is simpler and lives in one place — a failure inside the scheduler keeps the completed prefix, a refusal before it writes nothing.

**What the review checked and found correct**, recorded so it is not re-derived: every reference-table row recomputed independently and reproducing bit for bit; the `800` and not `1600` in the normalized-Elo scale; the Wald bound orientation, distinguished from a sign flip by an asymmetric error-rate case; the degenerate predicate sound at every reachable sample size, with the first spurious positive variance only beyond 1e15 observations and failing SAFE (toward refusal) when it comes; no LLR obtainable from a zero-variance sample; the seat-to-engine map correct in all four combinations; the turn cap off by exactly nothing; every path from worker count, completion order or clock into the verdict block enumerated and none found; and no swallowed error on any decision path — flips never; this line is history, and the lines it describes are the record.

D-172: The referee frames the exchange, and a line the arena did not ask for is a forfeit. Two RED-TEAM exploits, one of them the worst defect this work package produced, and both fixed here. **The unsolicited line.** The channel under the referee is a plain queue of lines and the protocol has no request identifier to match an answer to its question (D-2 pins the verb set), so a line an engine volunteers is not noise: it is read as the answer to the NEXT `go`, asked from a position the engine was never shown. Reproduced with a nine-line script engine that answers one `go` with two `bestmove` lines: the second was replayed as that engine's move two turns later, and the game finished as an ordinary `p1_win` counted into `n`, into `distinct_n`, into its pentanomial bucket and into the sample — with nothing anywhere in the report to say its move list is not what either engine intended. That is precisely "a number that is not a measurement" (CLAUDE.md rule 6), and it needs no malice: any engine build that ever emits a second `bestmove` — a buffering slip, a stray retry, a ponder racing the answer — silently corrupts every later turn of that game. The fix is a queue-emptiness check at both ends of every exchange, before the question and immediately after the `bestmove`, each asking only what has ALREADY arrived so that no wall-clock decision enters the referee (D-159). The residual limit is stated in the code rather than implied: a line arriving late enough could still be mistaken for the next answer, and no framing this protocol offers can close that; what is closed is every engine that has spoken by the time it is asked again, which is the reachable case. **The over-long line.** The read cap handed its truncated chunk over as though it were a complete line, so an engine streaming endless bytes beginning `info ` was read as an endless run of legitimate progress reports and the watchdog that fires on silence never got the chance to — measured at 2450 ms against a 400 ms `hang_timeout_ms`, with an ordinary `arena_report` written at the end rather than an abandoned one. A line over the cap is now its own outcome and forfeits by name; it is a forfeit rather than an abandonment because writing a megabyte with no newline is a deterministic wrong answer, which is the class D-159 says may be adjudicated — flips never.

D-173: `[sprt]` error rates are refused when they make a Wald boundary non-finite, and every float in a refusal or a summary is width-bounded. RED-TEAM's third exploit: `alpha > 0.0` admits subnormals, `ln((1 - beta)/alpha)` overflows, and `alpha = 1e-320` produced `bounds h0 -2.995732274 h1 inf` inside the verdict block — a non-numeric field in the machine-readable report, an H1 that can never be crossed, and therefore a silently mis-calibrated one-sided test that exited ZERO. Validation now computes the boundaries and refuses an impossible document rather than clamping it, which is what every other bound in that file does (D-18). The second half is smaller and real: `Display` on an f64 spells a subnormal out in full, so the refusal itself and the summary's bounds line ran to several hundred characters on one line; both now render in exponent form. Recorded as its own line rather than folded into D-172 because the two have different shapes — one is a protocol defect, this is a schema hole — flips never.

D-174: Records the WP-1.2b RED-TEAM round, including what it could not reach, so that unexplored surface is not later mistaken for cleared surface. Three exploits confirmed and fixed (D-172, D-173); the first was severe enough that it, not any design question, was this work package's most dangerous defect. What the round tried and the code correctly refused, which is the coverage evidence: an already-won opening (refused through `PositionSpec::replay`, so by shared rules code rather than by the arena); a genuine lattice-symmetry duplicate opening, refused by name — and worth noting, a hand-guessed "negate q" is NOT a lattice symmetry and was correctly accepted as distinct, which is a property of the group and not a miss; `bestmove 999999,999999`, which fails i16 parsing and forfeits as a bad bestmove; an openings body with no trailing newline; `hang_timeout_ms` at `u64::MAX`, which does not overflow an `Instant`; `turn_cap` and `openings_take` at their extremes, both typo-ceilinged before any arithmetic; and report-block truncation by an injected `# timing` line, which is structurally impossible because every line the arena sees came from a `read_until` on a newline, so engine text cannot contain one. The variance-cancellation attack was pushed further than REVIEW-impl took it and independently confirmed safe: all bucket scores are dyadic with denominator at most four, so a mathematically degenerate sample computes variance as exactly zero for every count below 2^53, and the first spurious non-zero appears at 9007199254740973 observations against a schema ceiling of two million — and it fails toward refusal rather than toward a tiny positive that would inflate the statistic. **NOT reached, and therefore not cleared:** a four-thousand-worker stress run with its zombie and file-descriptor accounting, and whether a panic in one worker poisons a mutex and hangs the scope; NUL bytes and invalid UTF-8 in an engine's output; `pistolok` sent twice; an engine ignoring `quit`; an engine closing stdin but not stdout; and a grandchild holding the pipe open past the direct child's exit. The first is a real gap in a way the others are less likely to be, because the concurrency surface is where a wrong verdict could still hide and it is the one surface no test in this crate exercises above four workers — flips when a second RED-TEAM pass covers the concurrency surface, which WP-1.3's first real run over the full book will motivate anyway.

D-175: A SEEDED RANDOM OPENING BOOK, and it is the PRIMARY book every SPRT runs over. OPERATOR RULING, and it supersedes nothing: `openings_v1.txt` is retained unchanged as the realism cross-check suite, and what this adds is a second book with different properties. `random_openings_v1.txt` holds 500 five-stone openings, each P1's stone at the origin and then P2's two and P1's two, sampled inside hex-distance 5 of the origin under a recorded seed and folded by the same canonical key WP-1.2a dedupes with (D-137). Three reasons it is primary. The research report's Deliverable 4 prescribes synthetic openings and the corpus book was the deviation, not this. Pairing already neutralises whatever per-opening bias any one of these carries, because both engines play both seats of every opening — so an opening being "unfair" costs a pair nothing, which is exactly the property a curated human book is *bought* for and does not need to be. And the supply of distinct games is unbounded here: the corpus book holds 1591 canonical openings and the corpus that produced it is finite, while this file's parameters can be asked for more of, which is the constraint CLAUDE.md rule 6's distinct-n reporting eventually runs into. **The stone count is a TURN-BOUNDARY count and 4 is a named refusal, not a rounding.** A turn places two stones (game rule 3), so an even count names a position no game is ever *at* — it is halfway through a turn — and `k_stones = 4` is refused as mid-turn rather than as unsupported, because those are two different complaints and only one of them would be answered by widening the set. The set is {3, 5} and the default is 5: three stones is P1's opener and P2's reply and little else. **There is NO BALANCE FILTER at this k, and the reason is arithmetic rather than a judgement.** A turn places two stones, so a mate in one TURN needs four own stones already in a six-window, and a mate in one PLY needs five; at five stones the largest holding is three, so no position in this file holds a mate in one for either side and there is nothing for a filter to remove. That arithmetic is also what keeps this file a FIXTURE under rule 7 rather than a book under rule 8, by D-151's own test: no engine judgement went into it, and D-151 says in as many words that a balance-filtered book WOULD be a book. The filter question reopens the day k grows past five, and it reopens as a rule-8 question and not only as a curation one. **Review scope**, recorded because it is narrower than the Process section's default: one fresh-context REVIEW-impl, no REVIEW-design, and no RED-TEAM. RED-TEAM was judged not required for this generator specifically — every position it emits is replayed through the same pistol-core path the arena and the engine use before it is written, so its output cannot be a position the rules refuse; and its only input is a committed config held to the same schema discipline as every other document under `configs/`, so there is no untrusted-input surface of the kind the WP-1.2b round attacked — flips if the tool ever reads a document it did not ship with, or if k grows past the arithmetic above.

D-176: `random-openings` is a THIRD binary in pistol-cli with a config document of its own, and this amends the crate map a third time (D-136 for `corpus-extract`, D-166 for `arena-stub-engine`) and D-168's document-kind list a second time. Not a mode of `corpus-extract`, and the deciding fact is that the two share no input: that tool's every path begins by reading an external corpus of human games and identifying it by SHA-256, and this one reads a committed TOML document and nothing else. They share no output and no code path either; what they share is the fixture *form*, and that is `corpus::emit`'s serialization discipline (D-147, D-148) rather than anything about a corpus. **Why this tool has a config where its sibling states that none reaches it.** `corpus-extract`'s argument is about an operator's TYPING — a fixture whose shape came from a command line is not reproducible from its own header — and it is not an argument against configuration. This document is committed, every field of it is echoed into the header of the file it produced, and a test regenerates that file from it and compares the bytes, so the four parameters are as pinned as constants would be and are visible in one document instead of spread through a source tree. It is a config rather than constants because the operator's ruling names `k_stones`, `max_radius` and `seed` as knobs, and `max_radius` in particular must be a knob that is visibly NOT `LEGAL_RADIUS`. pistol-cli grows serde, toml and serde_path_to_error to hold it; nothing on the engine's path in this crate reads TOML, and the crate already linked all three through pistol-engine, so the shipping binary gains no byte and no new transitive surface. That growth broke a recorded property and the breakage is recorded rather than quietly absorbed: `pistol_cli_manifest_names_only_core_and_engine` asserted the crate's WHOLE dependency list, and the scanner beside it said in its own doc comment that this crate has no TOML dependency. The test now asserts two things instead of one, because only one of them is a rule — the pistol-* subset is still exactly {core, engine}, which is CLAUDE.md rule 11's seam and is unmoved, and the full list is a ledger whose only job is that a fourth entry cannot arrive unremarked. That ledger claim was FALSE when it was first written and REVIEW-impl proved it so: the manifest scanner under all three shape tests turned itself off at any `[`-line it did not recognise, so a table-form `[dependencies.pistol-search]` added pistol-search to pistol-cli and left every assertion green — the rule half, not only the ledger half. The hole predates this work and the scanner backed the old assertion too, but this line is what made it load bearing, so it is closed here — and closed as a CLASS rather than a spelling, which the first fix was not. Recognising the table form left `[target.'cfg(unix)'.dependencies]` open, and a fourth spelling would have left a fifth: the scan now RECOGNISES two forms and REFUSES any other section header that names dependencies, so a manifest it cannot read is a red test rather than a green one. It fires on nothing in this workspace today, which is the point — it fires the day someone writes a spelling it does not know. dev-dependencies and build-dependencies stay excluded deliberately, because they do not ship. A guard with a door in it is worse than no guard, because it is cited. The scanner stays a scan for a reason that survives: a manifest test that parsed manifests with the parser under test would be reading the workspace through one of the things it polices. `tools/config_check.sh` learns the fourth kind, told apart by the name `random_openings_*.toml`, and the gate now says in its own header why a new kind must be named there the day it is committed: the fallback is "engine config", so an unrecognised document is not skipped, it is checked against the wrong schema and refused for every key it lacks. Also here, and smaller: the `--name value` grammar both curation binaries take moved into `pistol_cli::flags`, for the reason `count` gives for numbers — a rule with two implementations can hold two answers, and "unknown flag" is exactly the kind of message that drifts. `corpus::emit` was left where it is rather than being lifted out of the `corpus` module to serve two callers; that is one import reaching across, considered and declined as churn against a just-landed tree — flips at a third consumer.

D-177: The generation procedure, pinned here because every clause of it is a reason the file has these bytes and not others. **The PRNG is SplitMix64, reimplemented rather than depended on**, for the reason pistol-core is std-only: a fixture's bytes must not move because someone else's crate changed a constant or a default algorithm. What makes a reimplementation safe is an oracle, and this one has a published stream — the reference implementation's output from state 0 — which `random_openings_rng_tests.rs` pins it against. Every operation is `wrapping_*` on `u64`, so the stream is identical on every target and under D-127's release overflow checks. **Index sampling is by rejection**, not `% bound`: the modulus alone leans on the low residues by one part in `2^64 / bound`, invisible at a 91-cell ball and still a thumb on the scale of a book whose whole purpose is to be unbiased. At any bound this schema allows the rejection branch is unreachable — under one part in `2^57` — so it is tested at a bound where it is not, and what the test pins is the semantics: the discarded words are gone from the stream, not folded. **One word per stone.** A stone is drawn from the cells of the ball this candidate has not used yet, rather than from the whole ball with a redraw on a hit; the distribution is the same, there is no loop, and the stream's position after a candidate does not depend on how that candidate came out. Turn 1 is placed at the origin and never drawn (game rule 3). **The dedupe key is `canonical_form` over the twelve lattice symmetries** — D-137's key, which is also the key the arena's openings READER refuses a duplicate opening by, and deliberately NOT the key it counts distinct GAMES by: D-163 keys a game on `canonical_sequence` precisely because a position's canonical form would merge two different games that reached the same stones. An earlier draft of this line said the opposite and is corrected here rather than left standing, because D-163 exists to correct that exact confusion and a record that reintroduces it is worse than one that never addressed it — the code was right throughout; only this sentence was wrong — and a collision discards the WHOLE candidate and draws the next, a resample rule that is a function of the draws made so far and of nothing else. A pool that cannot supply the book refuses with the measurement in hand rather than writing a short one, because a sample size nobody chose is not a measurement (rule 6); the consecutive-collision limit that does this can only ever decide *whether* a run refuses and never what a successful run wrote, which is why it is a named constant and not a fifth config field. **Emission is generation order**, deliberately: the draws are independent, so a prefix of this file is already a sample, and sorting by anything would make a prefix a slice of whatever was sorted on — D-143's argument, in a book that gets it for free. **`max_radius` is never reconciled with `LEGAL_RADIUS`.** It has its own typo ceiling and may be set past 8, at which point a drawn stone can land beyond eight of every stone on the board; that is its own named refusal, and it is never a silent redraw, because redrawing would quietly turn `max_radius` into "somewhere inside this, mostly" and reconciling the two radii by hand is the conflation CLAUDE.md rule 2 forbids. **And the regeneration test.** D-152 found committed fixtures whose bytes the build could no longer produce, because every test read the committed file and none compared it against fresh output; that hole is closed by construction here rather than by care, since this book's only input is a committed config, so `random_openings_v1_is_what_this_build_produces` is a test and not an errand with an external corpus in it. Editing the header prose without regenerating is a red test, which is precisely what could not be seen before. Recorded from the mutation round, in a separate worktree, and corrected where REVIEW-impl found the first account of it inaccurate: removing the dedupe, the origin's reservation, the ball's boundary, the emission order, the seed, the mid-turn/unsupported ordering, the schema-version equality and `deny_unknown_fields` each turns a named test red. Removing the consecutive-collision limit does NOT — it HANGS, because the test that covers exhaustion then loops forever, so CI would stop rather than fail; the first draft of this line called it a red test and that was wrong. Giving rule 5 its own named refusal was a change the round FORCED: with the guard folded into a generic placement error, deleting it changed nothing any test could see. Two mutations survive and are named rather than left for the next reader to find, both of them in `spell` and both of the same kind — the comparison of the re-read position's key against the generated one, and the comparison of the re-read move list against the one written. Each is a belt-and-braces check with no fault this suite can inject, and the reason that is acceptable rather than dead code is that a mutation which reorders stones ACROSS turns, changing their colours, is caught by the regeneration test with both checks disabled — so neither is ever the sole detector of anything. A third survivor was NOT acceptable and was closed: an off-by-one in the rejection zone (`u64::MAX % bound` for `2^64 mod bound`) biases one index by one word in `2^64`, which no sample this tool draws could ever show, so the arithmetic is now its own function and is asserted against a 128-bit oracle over a table of bounds. That is the shape any unreachable-by-measurement invariant should take here.

D-178: Real arena runs cap `n_workers` at 4 until a dedicated concurrency pass covers the surface D-174 lists as not reached, and the cap lives in WP-1.3's pre-registration rather than in code. In the pre-registration because it is an experimental protocol and not a property of the runner: the config field is a knob whose safe range is a fact about how well the surface has been tested, which changes when the testing changes, and a ceiling compiled into `validate.rs` would have to be edited by ADR every time it moved. Four because that is the highest worker count any test in the crate exercises — `stop_tests.rs` compares a crossing sample at one worker and at four — so it is the boundary of what has actually been shown, not a number chosen for comfort. What is uncovered above it is D-174's own list: zombie and file-descriptor accounting at scale, and whether a panic in one worker poisons a mutex and hangs the scope. A wrong verdict is the failure mode this guards, which is why it is a hard cap on real runs and not advice — flips when a second RED-TEAM pass covers the concurrency surface, which is the same event D-174 names.

D-179: WP-1.3's pre-registration states the verdict level — pair-level GSPRT per D-154, or game-level — IN WRITING before the first game of the first experiment, and no run may change it afterwards. The Process section already forbids post-hoc threshold moves and this line makes its application to D-154 explicit, because D-154 is exactly the kind of choice that invites a quiet re-reading: it demotes the game-level LLR to a reported diagnostic, and a report that carries BOTH numbers is a report where reading the other one after the fact requires no code change, no config change and no visible act. Naming the level in the pre-registration turns that from an unlogged choice into a contradiction of a document — flips never; the rule is the existing Process rule and this line is its application.

D-180: The desync residual WP-1.2b's RED-TEAM left open is ACCEPTED while both ends of every arena match are pistol CLI builds. D-172 closed every engine that has finished speaking by the time it is asked again, and stated the limit it cannot close: the protocol has no request identifier (D-2 pins the verb set), so a line arriving late enough could still be read as the answer to the next question. What makes that acceptable is not that it is unlikely, it is that both ends are the same synchronous-by-design program (D-2): a pistol build answers exactly one line per question and emits nothing unbidden, so the late line has no source. The ruling flips the day any non-pistol engine connects to the arena — which is separately forbidden, and this line exists so the boundary is findable when someone proposes lifting that — at which point the fix is a protocol-level request identifier echoed in the answer, not a wider queue check.

D-181: Records the random-openings REVIEW-impl round, because two of its findings were sentences in D-176 and D-177 that the code did not support, one was a guard that had a door in it, and a reader of those two lines should know which clauses were corrected and why. Fresh context, against a named revision, in a separate worktree. **The guard with a door.** The manifest scanner behind all three workspace-shape tests set `inside = (line == "[dependencies]")` on every `[`-line, so the TABLE form of a dependency turned the scan off and its body was skipped: `[dependencies.pistol-search]` added pistol-search to pistol-cli, cargo resolved and built against it, and every assertion stayed green — including the one this session had just relabelled as CLAUDE.md rule 11's seam. Reproduced in both spellings, fixed by recognising the table form, and both are red now. The hole predates this work; what is new is D-176 citing it. **The record that reintroduced a corrected confusion.** D-177's first draft said the generator's dedupe key "is also the key the arena counts distinct games by (D-163)" — and D-163 says the opposite in as many words, because it is the line that corrected exactly this in the arena's own design. The code was right throughout: the generator folds openings by `canonical_form`, which is what WP-1.2a does and what the arena's openings READER does, while the arena's distinct-GAME key is `canonical_sequence`. Corrected in the ADR and in the test comment that had copied it. **A validator on one of two doors.** `generate` is public, every field of the config is public, and validation lived only in `parse`, so a struct literal reached the generator with any stone count and any radius — including k = 7, where a side holds four stones and D-175's no-balance-filter arithmetic stops holding. `generate` now revalidates, and the `unwrap_or(i16::MAX)` that would have silently clamped an absurd radius is an `unreachable!` naming the invariant instead. **Coverage the round added.** The binary was executed by no test and no gate — `corpus-extract` is driven through `CARGO_BIN_EXE_` at seven sites and this one at none — so its exit codes, its refusals, its `--help`, and the staged-then-renamed write that must not replace a good book with a partial one are now pinned by a CLI test file, including a two-PROCESS byte-identity check matching `tools/determinism.sh`'s shape. A second pass over that file closed the last branch nothing reached, which was the cleanup after a rename that failed: a directory standing at the book's own name lets the staged write succeed and the rename fail, which is the only way to reach it, and what the test asserts is that the staged file does not outlive the run — a half-finished output left beside a name that does not exist yet being the thing the staging exists to prevent. The write-failure paths are chosen to be root-safe: a permission bit stops meaning anything when tests run as root, and a directory standing where a file must go does not. Three of the seven operator-named tests read only the committed fixture, which its own digest already pins, so their comments claimed of the generator what they asserted of the file: the radius test now generates at two further radii and catches the ball's boundary mutation, which it previously did not. And the rejection-zone arithmetic is now checked against a 128-bit oracle (D-177). **What the round checked and found correct**, recorded so it is not re-derived: the sampler's uniformity, by chi-squared over a million draws and by an independent reimplementation in another language that reproduced the committed book's opening lines from the seed alone; the SplitMix64 stream against the published reference; the rejection-zone identity proved at bound 1, 2, `2^63 + 1` and `u64::MAX`; the colour assignment re-derived over all 500 lines; no position won, illegal, mid-turn or duplicated; no nondeterminism on any path into the bytes; every failure path leaving no partial or stale file; the mate-in-one arithmetic including that four-in-a-six-window is the right threshold for a turn and five for a ply; the `flags` extraction character-identical in every refusal message; and the arena's own loader reading the finished book, 500 openings with the in-band digest verified — which is a fact worth having written down, because nothing in the tree asserts it (see below) — flips never; this line is history, and the lines it describes are the record.

D-182: NOTHING IN THE TREE PINS THAT THE ARENA CAN LOAD THE BOOK D-175 CALLS PRIMARY, and that gap is recorded rather than closed, because closing it means touching pistol-arena and this session's scope forbids it. The two serializations are written in different crates — pistol-cli emits the file, pistol-arena's `openings::load` reads it — and every property the reader requires is asserted today only on the WRITER's side: the `# body_sha256` header and body offset, a payload of position tails and no stray `#` line, a uniform turn count, and no two openings equal up to a lattice symmetry. That is not nothing, and it is not the same as the reader having read it. REVIEW-impl loaded the committed book through `pistol_arena::openings::load` by hand and it succeeded — 500 openings, in-band digest verified, no duplicate refusal — so the compatibility is a fact as of this revision and not a hope; what is missing is anything that would notice the day one side's serialization moves. The fix is one test in pistol-arena and belongs with WP-1.3, which is where the arena is next opened and where the pre-registration must name the book anyway (D-178, D-179) — flips the moment WP-1.3 starts, and this line is the reminder that it is owed.

D-183: D-182 IS CLOSED. `arena_loads_primary_book_with_digest` loads the committed `random_openings_v1.txt` through `pistol_arena::openings::load` and asserts 500 openings, the in-band body digest by value, and the three-turn opening length rule 3 gives a five-stone position. It is a cross-crate test because the gap was cross-crate: pistol-cli writes the file and pistol-arena reads it, and every property the reader requires was asserted only on the writer's side — the `# body_sha256` header and the body offset under it, a payload of position tails with no stray `#` line, one turn count for every opening, and no two openings equal up to a lattice symmetry. Asserting those where they are produced is not the same as the reader having read them, and D-175 makes this file the book every SPRT runs over, so a drift between the two serializations must be a red test rather than a failed experiment. The digest is asserted BY VALUE and not merely by loading successfully, because `load` verifies the body against the header's own claim and refuses a mismatch — so a load that returned `Ok` already proves the file self-consistent, and what the constant adds is that the bytes are the ones this test was written against: a book regenerated under a different seed would still be internally consistent and would still load. It goes in `openings_tests.rs` rather than a new file because that module is already "the openings fixture is verified against its own in-band digest", which is what this is. **Review judgment, recorded because CLAUDE.md's Process section would otherwise require a round**: none beyond `tools/ci.sh`. This is a single load-path test over a fixture that is already replay-validated — every position in it goes through pistol-core before it is written (D-177) and through `PositionSpec::replay` again inside `load` — so the test adds an assertion about a file whose contents are not in question, and there is no new code path for a reviewer to attack. That judgment is scoped to THIS test; it does not extend to WP-1.3, whose first real run is a strength claim under rule 6 — flips if this test ever grows a second responsibility.

D-184: The corpus fixtures are regenerated to correct a header pointer that named a file which does not exist, and the regeneration is recorded because a fixture re-pin that changes a digest must say what moved. Both `openings_v1.txt` and `bench_positions_v1.txt` said "Pinned by SHA-256 in `crates/pistol-cli/tests/corpus_output_tests.rs`"; the constants live in `corpus_document_tests.rs`, and that file has never existed under the other name in any committed revision. A header that points at nothing is a rule-3 defect in the document rule 7 exists to pin — and it is the same class D-152 records, a fixture whose prose stopped matching the tree, found this time by reading rather than by a gate. The correction is one line in `corpus/documents.rs` and the evidence that it is only that: the corpus was verified by digest (`b2fe61eb…`, matching the header it was about to rewrite) BEFORE regenerating, the outputs were written to a scratch directory and diffed against the committed ones rather than over them, and the diff is exactly one line per file. Both payload digests are unchanged — `e5165ce1…` and `d62bde75…` — so no position, no ordering and no curation number moved; only the two whole-file pins did, to `5ccc3dc0…` and `931c50b1…`. The reason this could be done now and not when it was found is that the corpus is an external artifact and is never committed (rule 8), so a session without it can correct the source and cannot produce the bytes — flips nothing; the practice this confirms is that a fixture regeneration states its input's digest, diffs before it installs, and stops if anything but the intended lines moves.

D-185: A gate or test claim in any report cites the gate's own log output, never a wrapper's exit status. Added to CLAUDE.md's Workflow section, and it is here because it was learned rather than designed: in the session that landed WP-1.2a, WP-1.2b and the random book, `tools/ci.sh` was run as `./tools/ci.sh > log 2>&1; echo "EXIT=$?"; tail log`, and the harness's completion notice reported the exit status of the COMPOUND command — that is, of `tail` — which is zero whatever the gates did. Two runs were reported green to the operator that had in fact failed on `cargo test`, and the failure was real: a shape test that pins pistol-cli's dependency list. Nothing about the gate was wrong; the reading of it was. The rule names the log rather than the exit code in general because the log is the artifact the gate itself produces — `ci: all gates passed` is written by the thing that knows, while an exit status is whatever the last process in a pipeline happened to return — and a project whose strength claims are all instrument readings (rule 6) should not accept a weaker standard of evidence about its own gates than about its engine — flips never.

D-186: WP-1.3 IS PRE-REGISTERED IN docs/experiments/wp13_prereg.md AND IN ITS FOUR COMMITTED RUN CONFIGS, at revision eb6ea93, before the first game and the first profile; the operator's runbook is the source and every blank it left is filled there, together with four it did not have. The numbers that are not simply the runbook's recommendation are here because each is a choice. **`elo1 = 25` normalized Elo, deviating from the research report's Deliverable 4 range of 3-5 and from the runbook's recommended 5**, for an arithmetic reason and not a preference: `random_openings_v1.txt` supplies 500 openings, every opening is exactly one pair and the game cap is derived as twice `openings_take` (D-157), so 500 pairs is the whole sample available, and two independent calculations agree on what that resolves — the report's own `games ~= 640000/elo1^2` solves to 25.3 at 1000 games, and `conclusion.rs::confidence`, which is `1.96 / (NELO_TO_T * sqrt(2) * sqrt(pairs))` and therefore a function of the pair count ALONE with the observed scores never entering it, is +/-21.5 normalized Elo there. At the pair-level GSPRT this crate implements, elo1 = 5 accepts H1 only at an observed +73.6 and H0 only at -68.6, so it would print a verdict about a five-Elo difference beside an interval four times wider and could conclude inside the book only on a ~70-Elo effect; at 25 the thresholds are +26.7 and -1.7 and the verdict and the interval say the same thing. Rejected, and recorded because this is re-openable: (a) elo1 = 5 as recommended, on the arithmetic above; (b) elo1 = 30, which is marginally better powered — it reaches an H0 verdict at a true tie inside the book at 395 pairs where 25 needs 569 — rejected only because 25 is where the report's formula and the instrument's own interval both land, and a bound derived from the instrument is easier to defend than one tuned for its own power; (c) regenerating the book at ~12800 openings so elo1 = 5 is powered, which D-175 anticipated by making the supply unbounded, rejected as a work package of its own plus ~3.5 days of games at four workers, and reconsidered after this run rather than before it. **The budget is fixed nodes = 50000**, from a recorded calibration probe that is not part of any sample: 4.9 s per game and 2.4 s per side meets the runbook's single-digit-seconds-per-side criterion, a second deepening iteration completes in some games rather than in none (25000) or at ten times the cost (100000), and the probe also measured what a fixed-node instrument is worth — the first iteration is uninterruptible by D-74's design, so one position spent 104448 nodes against a 25000 budget, which makes node-matching approximate and is why the per-side compute lines are read rather than assumed. **`turn_cap = 40` and `hang_timeout_ms = 120000` are pre-registered although the runbook has no blank for them**, because `turn_cap` is not statistically inert — D-157 measured capped games accelerating the LLR toward H1 — and a knob left to run time is a knob nobody registered; 40 is three times the longest of sixty probe games, none of which capped. **And the radius-2 configuration sits in `engine_a`, which is the REVERSE of the runbook's lettering, deliberately**: the arena's statistic is engine A's score, so `elo1 > 0` states "A is stronger than B" and nothing else, and had the committed radius-3 config taken slot A as the runbook's "A = committed config" reads, the tool would have tested the opposite hypothesis to the pre-registered direction and the error would have surfaced only as a sign nobody questioned. The runbook's citation of an "A-2 ADR" for the primary book is to a line that does not exist; the ruling is D-175, pinned cross-crate by D-183, and that is what the documents cite — flips only by a NEW pre-registration commit and a re-run, never by an edit to the registered one; an inconclusive result at the cap is a result and leaves radius 3 committed, because the incumbent wins ties.

D-187: THE PRIMARY BOOK IS EXTENDED FROM 500 OPENINGS TO 2000, BY EDITING `configs/random_openings_v1.toml` IN PLACE AND REGENERATING, amending D-175's "holds 500 five-stone openings" and the count D-183's cross-crate test asserts. The reason is that the book is the entire sample a paired SPRT can draw on, so it does not merely size a run — it fixes the design's error rates, and at 500 openings the rates WP-1.3 declared could not be delivered. Measured on this crate's own `Sample` and `crossing` over 40 000 simulated runs per truth: at 500 pairs, `elo0 = 0`, `elo1 = 25`, `alpha = beta = 0.05` achieves alpha 0.030 and power **0.569** against its own alternative, because the LLR needs 569 pairs to reach a boundary on drift alone and the book ran out at 500; at 2000 pairs the same bounds achieve alpha 0.049 and power 0.945. A declared beta the design cannot deliver is worse than a smaller claim, and no `elo1` fixes it at 500 — 95% power there needs about 1480 pairs, and an `elo1` large enough to be powered at 500 pushes the Wald approximation anti-conservative. **It costs almost nothing, which is what makes it the cheap fix rather than the expensive one**: the sequential test stops when it has an answer, so quadrupling the cap raises the EXPECTED pairs played from 374 to about 520 — some six minutes at four workers — and the cap binds only on the runs that need it. **In place rather than as a `v2` book, for two reasons.** The generator hard-names its output (`FILE_NAME`) and `document.rs` embeds the v1 prose into every header it writes, so a second book is a code change to a reviewed generator, two fixtures to keep in step, and a superseding line against D-175; while editing the one number the config exists to hold is precisely the operation D-177 built the machinery for, and it needs no code at all. And the edit is provably an EXTENSION rather than a replacement: emission is generation order and the draws are independent (D-177), so the committed 500 openings are the first 500 lines of the new book byte for byte — verified, and now pinned by `a_shorter_book_is_a_prefix_of_the_committed_one`, which regenerates a 500-opening book from the committed parameters and compares it line by line against the committed file, so the day that property stops holding is a red test rather than a silently discarded sample. Three pins moved and each was caught by its own test rather than by care: the whole-file digest `RANDOM_OPENINGS_V1_SHA256`, the config's `n_openings` assertion, and D-183's `arena_loads_primary_book_with_digest` (count and in-band body digest); `random_openings_v1_is_what_this_build_produces` passed throughout, which is D-152's hole staying closed. Rejected: leaving the book at 500 and declaring the 0.569 power honestly, which ships a design whose stated purpose — deciding whether radius 2 replaces radius 3 — is discarded 43% of the time it should fire; and a `v2` book, whose case would become the right one the moment a published claim depended on the 500-opening bytes, which today none does because no run has been made — flips if a future design needs a different `n`, which moves this line rather than the fixture's name, or if a result is ever published against these bytes, after which a versioned second book is the honest shape and this line is the argument for it.

D-188: THE WP-1.3 PRE-REGISTRATION IS AMENDED TO REVISION 2 BEFORE ANY RUN, superseding the parts of D-186 named below; no game and no profile was run under revision 1, so this is the review window closing rather than a threshold moving. Three fresh-context rounds attacked the document committed at `23f14f0` — two REVIEW-design and one RED-TEAM — and what they took down was not the arithmetic, every figure of which reproduced exactly, but the inference drawn from it and three claims about what the tooling does. **Withdrawn from D-186, sentence by sentence.** (a) The derivation of `elo1 = 25` from the research report's `games ~= 640000/elo1^2`: that expression sizes the sample at which the LLR's EXPECTED value first reaches a boundary — a roughly 50%-completion heuristic — and reading it as a power formula chose a half-powered design by construction, which D-187 measures and fixes by moving the CAP rather than the alternative. (b) "a true tie runs to the cap and reports the interval instead", which was the modal outcome only on the noiseless path: at 500 pairs a true tie accepted H0 with probability 0.57 before the cap. (c) The count "FOUR COMMITTED RUN CONFIGS", which is three arena configs and one engine config. (d) The `elo1 = 5` true-tie row, 14 218 pairs and not 14 217. **And four claims about the tooling that were wrong rather than merely imprecise.** The workers justification cited D-174 as having CLEARED four workers; D-174 lists the concurrency surface under "NOT reached, and therefore not cleared" and predicts that WP-1.3's first full-book run would motivate the pass that clears it — which is what happened, WP-1.3's own RED-TEAM round getting byte-identical verdict blocks at 1, 2, 4 and 8 workers over the full 1591-opening book through a real early stop, where nothing in this repository had previously run the arena above two. The Deliverable-4 table promised that the eval weight table's digest "stands in" for a net hash; nothing digests that file, and two workspaces differing only in it produce byte-identical `experiment_sha256` and every other recorded identity while `nelo_pair` moves by 98 and the first-player rate by 25 points — recorded as a named limit in the pre-registration's §9 and as a code work package, not papered over. H1's profile target `Position::static_score_after` does not exist as a symbol in the deployment build, and the stated fallback of everything inclusive under `ordering::order` would have swept in the allocation and the sort that H2 separately counts, making H1 near-self-confirming for a hypothesis that gates D-110's `Eval::delta`; the target is now the three `Eval` callees behind `Box<dyn Eval>`, which cannot be inlined. And the claim that an r2 win on nodes would be a win on time was refuted by the pre-registration's own probe table at its own budget, so the direction is now read off the run rather than asserted in advance. **Added rather than corrected:** a 100-pair floor on the H1 ACTION, because at this alternative the smallest crossing is ten pairs and D-156 declined a floor when it was thirty-three; the decisive-pair count as a required ADR field, because a normalized-Elo bar is set by the run's own tie rate and 494 tied pairs beside six swept ones crosses H1; a run order of 3a before 1, since a self-match on the same book, budget and worker count is a strictly stronger determinism gate than the four-opening smoke and a non-degenerate result there invalidates Run 1's verdict unit; a rule that no `configs/` document is edited and no engine binary rebuilt while a run is live, because digests are taken once and engines are respawned from disk per game, and a swap eighteen seconds into a live run produced exit 0 and a report attesting the old config; and named `.matchlog` output paths outside the repository, because `--out` refuses an existing file only at dispatch and a report named `.txt` passes both `.gitignore` and `tools/artifact_check.sh` — flips never as an amendment; a change after Run 3a's first game is a new pre-registration and a re-run, not a further line here.

D-189: WP-1.3 RUN 3a — THE FIRST PLAYER WINS 61.8% OF DISTINCT GAMES ON THE PRIMARY BOOK AT THE 50 000-NODE INSTRUMENT, 1236 of 2000 (2472 of 4000 played), Wilson 95% [0.5965, 0.6390], which is 10.6 sigma from an even game. This is the number CLAUDE.md's rule 6 and the research report's Deliverable 4 both ask for and that the opening corpus could not give, because a corpus's own first-player rate is confounded by which humans were playing (D-145). **It contradicts the research report's stated prior and the conflict is reported rather than averaged away**, per that report's own instruction: its Caveats section reasons that the reduced fork density on 3 axes "plausibly tilts toward the DEFENDER" and this measurement tilts the other way, hard. **It is a property of THIS INSTRUMENT and not a constant of the game**, which is why the budget is part of the claim and not a footnote: `configs/instrument_v0.toml` both seats, candidate radius 3, fixed nodes 50 000, `turn_cap` 40, four workers, book `random_openings_v1.txt` at body digest `7b1b3a99...`, `experiment_sha256 138048ad...`, per side 477 711 420 nodes over 11 060 searches with a deepest completed depth of 2 turns, 1.49 h wall. At this budget most searches complete one turn of depth and some complete two (docs/experiments/wp13_prereg.md 2c), so what is measured is the first player's advantage against an opponent that mostly cannot see the reply, and a deeper instrument is entitled to a different number. **The sample is the 2000 DISTINCT games and not the 4000 played**: two identical deterministic engines play the same game from either seat, so both games of a pair are the same game and quoting an interval on 4000 would halve a width the run did not earn. **This run was also the package's determinism gate and it held exactly**: `n 4000`, `distinct_n 2000`, all 2000 pairs in bucket `p2`, zero capped, zero forfeits, both sides on identical node counts to the node, verdict `inconclusive_degenerate` — the answer the determinism law forces for a self-match (D-156), and the reason Run 1's pair-level verdict unit (D-154) stands on measured ground rather than on the four-opening smoke. It is not comparable with Run 3b's rate and the two are never averaged: this book samples openings uniformly, while the corpus book's are the ones humans reached and D-145 measured those lopsided, so 3b estimates the first player's advantage CONDITIONED on a human-reached opening — flips on a different instrument, which is a new measurement and a new line rather than an amendment to this one; a Stage-2 eval or a Stage-1 threat search deep enough to see replies is the most likely thing to move it, and balancing the opening book is a Stage-5 question this number is an input to.

D-190: WP-1.3 RUN 1 — CANDIDATE RADIUS 2 BEATS RADIUS 3 AT THE 50 000-NODE INSTRUMENT, CONFIRMED ON A DISJOINT SAMPLE, so the pre-registered H1 action fires and radius 2 becomes the committed candidate policy — landed by its own config commit after all four WP-1.3 runs complete, per the pre-registration's rule that no `configs/` document moves while a run of this package is live (docs/experiments/wp13_prereg.md 8). Run 1, primary book at body digest `7b1b3a99...`, `experiment_sha256 ac554c37...`: verdict `h1` at 37 pairs and 74 games, radius 2 winning 56 to 18, pentanomial 2/0/14/0/21 for 23 decisive pairs, `llr_pair` 3.0402 against a 2.9444 bound, `nelo_pair +210.87 ci95 +/-79.16`, no capped game and no forfeit. **The crossing was below the pre-registered 100-pair floor, so the action was withheld and the confirmatory run decided it**, which is the floor doing exactly the job it was added for: at this alternative the smallest possible crossing is ten pairs, and a config change resting on twenty games is not one this project should make. The confirmation is `configs/arena_wp13_r2_vs_r3_confirm.toml`, Run 1's document with the book and its size changed and nothing else — `openings_v1.txt`, 1591 openings, body digest `e5165ce1...`, `experiment_sha256 2084390b...` — chosen because both engines are deterministic in instrument mode, so re-running Run 1 reproduces Run 1 and confirms nothing, and because `openings_take` takes a prefix with no offset knob. It returned `h1` at 50 pairs and 100 games, radius 2 winning 70 to 30, pentanomial 4/0/22/0/24 for 28 decisive pairs, `nelo_pair +155.38 ci95 +/-68.10`. **Stated because it is the honest reading**: the confirmatory run also stopped short of 100 pairs, and the pre-registered condition it had to meet was "also crosses H1", which it did; the two disjoint samples together are 87 pairs, 174 games, 51 decisive pairs and 126 wins of 174 for radius 2, and their intervals overlap. Both intervals are optimistic, per the pre-registered reading: coverage at a sequential stop was measured at 0.868 against 0.978 for a run reaching the cap. **THE WIN IS NODE-MATCHED AND IS NOT A WALL-CLOCK WIN, and the pre-registration refused to assert the direction in advance for exactly this reason.** Radius 2 won Run 1 using 6.1% FEWER nodes and 1.90x the wall-clock (19 321 912 nodes in 732 595 ms against 20 573 453 in 384 783), and the confirmatory run reproduces the shape at 1.44x. The mechanism is the one measured before any game: at a fixed node budget radius 2 completes a second turn-iteration in 17 of the 24 bench positions where radius 3 manages 6, and a depth-1 iteration searches the mover's own turn without ever seeing the reply — so the narrower set buys depth, depth wins, and the extra depth is where the per-node time goes (nps collapses when a search reaches depth 2). This REFUTES the prior written into `configs/instrument_v0.toml`, that "radius 2 risks tactical blindness", at this instrument and at this instrument only. **What this decides and what it does not.** It decides the candidate policy at a fixed-node instrument, which is what the research report's recommendation 5 prescribes for exactly this comparison. It does NOT decide the policy at a fixed-TIME budget, and CLAUDE.md's design point is a wall-clock 0.5 s move: at equal time radius 2 would take roughly half the nodes it had here, and whether its depth advantage survives that is unmeasured and is not claimed. That comparison belongs with WP-1.4, which owns the movetime path (D-95) — flips on a deeper instrument, since nothing here predicts the ordering once Stage 1's threat-first generation supersedes the radius policy entirely (docs/ROADMAP.md WP-1.5), and flips on a time-matched SPRT, which is a different experiment and needs its own pre-registration.

D-191: WP-1.3 RUN 3b — ON HUMAN-REACHED OPENINGS THE FIRST PLAYER WINS 57.1% OF DISTINCT GAMES AT THE 50 000-NODE INSTRUMENT, 909 of 1591 (1818 of 3182 played), Wilson 95% [0.5469, 0.5955], 5.7 sigma from an even game; `experiment_sha256 378800a0...`, book `openings_v1.txt` at body digest `e5165ce1...`, `configs/instrument_v0.toml` both seats, four workers, per side 407 406 809 nodes over 9 287 searches, 1.57 h wall, zero capped and zero forfeits. **This number and D-189's 61.8% are NEVER AVERAGED and the difference between them is not a discrepancy**: they estimate different things by construction. D-189's book samples five-stone openings uniformly under a recorded seed, so it estimates the first player's advantage from an arbitrary position; this book's openings are the ones humans actually reached, they are seven stones and one turn deeper, and D-145 measured them lopsided in their own right — first-player rates from 0.10 to 0.91 across canonical classes with at least ten corpus games, 26 of 61 outside 0.35-0.65 — so this estimates the advantage CONDITIONED on a human-reached opening. That the conditioned number is the smaller of the two is a fact about which openings humans choose, not evidence that either measurement is wrong. **Both are properties of this instrument and neither is a constant of the game.** At 50 000 nodes most searches complete one turn of depth and some complete two, so both rates describe an opponent that mostly cannot see the reply; the pre-registration withdrew, before any game was played, an earlier claim that the probe had *measured* the rate moving with the budget, because ten paired openings cannot show that at any p below 0.5 — the caution survives and the observation did not. **What they agree on is the sign, and it is the interesting part**: the research report's Caveats reason that reduced fork density on 3 axes "plausibly tilts toward the DEFENDER", and both books, at 10.6 and 5.7 sigma, tilt the other way. Reported as a conflict rather than averaged into the prior, per that report's own instruction. **The determinism law held again**: `n 3182`, `distinct_n 1591`, all 1591 pairs in bucket `p2`, both sides on identical node counts, `inconclusive_degenerate` — the answer a self-match is forced to give (D-156), here at a second book and a different opening depth. Two reporting notes that cost nothing now and would cost a reader later: the `llr_game -8.24` on this report is far past its boundary and means nothing, because the verdict unit is the pair and D-154 makes the game-level statistic a diagnostic; and `first_player_wins` counts forfeited games as decided, so the zero in `forfeits` is what licenses reading this rate at all — flips on a different instrument, which is a new measurement and a new line; the Stage-5 balanced-book generator is the consumer of both numbers, and a threat search deep enough to answer a reply is the most likely thing to move either.

D-192: WP-1.3 RUN 2, HYPOTHESIS H1 — **CONFIRMED at 76.27% of pooled samples against a pre-registered threshold of 20%**, so D-76's eval apply/undo roundtrip in move ordering is this engine's hotspot by a margin that leaves nothing to argue about, and `Eval::delta` (D-110) is unlocked as its own work package with D-110's oracle test and a Hard-Rule-5 bench. The measurement, on operator hardware in a release build with `overflow-checks` on, fixed nodes 50 000 over both bands of `bench_positions_v1.txt`, `configs/instrument_v0.toml` at candidate radius 3 as the pre-registration pinned it regardless of Run 1's outcome: 24 810 samples pooled (14 544 early band, 10 266 late), of which 18 923 have a stack containing one of `<HandcraftedV0 as Eval>::{apply, undo, value}` *and* passing through `pistol_search::ordering::order` — 79.81% in the early band and 71.26% in the late. Attribution is by the amended rule and not by the one revision 1 wrote: `Position::static_score_after` does not survive as a symbol in this build (`nm -C | grep -c` returns 0, it is fully inlined), so the target is the three `Eval` callees, which sit behind `Box<dyn Eval>` and therefore cannot be inlined into `order`, counted only on stacks passing through `order` — which is what keeps H1's figure clear of the sort and the allocation that H2 counts. Context, since a hotspot is only meaningful against the whole: the eval roundtrip is on 85.62% of stacks anywhere, so ordering accounts for roughly nine tenths of it and the search's own `place`/`undo` for the remaining 9.35%; pooled SELF time is `Eval::undo` 28.80%, `Eval::apply` 24.66%, `windows_through`'s iterator 13.51%, `candidate_cells` 7.74%. **The profiling build DEVIATES from what the pre-registration described, and the deviation is recorded rather than hidden**: §5 said line tables would be added by environment override and that this "changes no codegen", but perf on this machine produced no usable call graphs from `--call-graph dwarf` at either an 8 KB or a 64 KB stack dump — every entry came back with `Children == Self` despite `HAVE_DWARF_UNWIND_SUPPORT` being on and the binary carrying `.eh_frame` and `.eh_frame_hdr` — so the profile was retaken with `-C force-frame-pointers=yes` and `--call-graph fp`, which DOES change codegen. Its cost was measured rather than assumed, at identical node counts since the engine is deterministic: +1.0% to +3.6% wall-clock across four positions, median about +2.8%, which cannot move a figure that cleared its threshold by 56 points — flips never as an adjudication; what it now gates is whether `delta()` actually wins its own bench, which is a different question and D-110's own oracle test is what keeps the answer honest.

D-193: WP-1.3 RUN 2, HYPOTHESIS H2 — **NOT CONFIRMED, at 0.29% of pooled samples against a pre-registered threshold of 10%**, a factor of thirty-four below the bar, so per-node allocation in `candidates.rs`/`ordering.rs` is not a hotspot, no fix is licensed, and by D-110's own construction the absence IS this line's answer. 71 samples of 24 810 have a stack containing an allocation entry point and passing through `candidates::candidate_cells` or `ordering::order`; allocation appears anywhere on only 0.30% of stacks. **The first pass of this adjudication produced 11.46% and would have CONFIRMED it, and the reason it was wrong is worth the sentence**: the pattern matching allocation frames included `alloc::alloc::`, which appears in these profiles overwhelmingly as the GENERIC PARAMETER `alloc::alloc::Global` inside `alloc::collections::btree::node::…` symbols — BTreeMap surgery in the eval's window map, reached from `ordering::order` through the very roundtrip H1 measures, and therefore eval work counted as allocation. Corrected to match actual allocation entry points only (`__rust_alloc`/`__rust_dealloc`/`__rust_realloc`, `alloc::alloc::{alloc,dealloc,realloc}`, `alloc::raw_vec`, and the libc allocator symbols), the figure falls to 0.29%. A threshold pre-registered before the numbers is no protection if the quantity measured against it is the wrong one, and this one was caught only because 11.46% sat suspiciously close to a 10% bar and the matched frames were listed rather than trusted. **What the profile DID surface, recorded and deliberately NOT adjudicated**: BTreeMap node operations appear on 23.21% of stacks and hold two of the six self-time leaders at 4.99% and 4.70%, i.e. `pistol_eval`'s `BTreeMap<Window, Counts>` is a real second-order cost. That is a THIRD hypothesis, and D-114 says in as many words that a third hypothesis means a new D-line and a new profile, never an addition to this one after the numbers are in — so it is written here as an observation for a future pre-registration and nothing is concluded from it — flips never for this profile; a future work package that re-registers the window map as its own hypothesis is the successor, and `Eval::delta` landing first may change that map's access pattern enough to make it a different question.

D-194: THE COMMITTED CANDIDATE POLICY IS RADIUS 2. `configs/instrument_v0.toml` moves from 3 to 2 and the argument that file used to carry — that radius 2 "risks tactical blindness" — is withdrawn rather than left standing beside the number that beat it. This is the pre-registered H1 action of WP-1.3 Run 1 firing (D-190), deliberately after all four runs completed, because the H1 action edits the document that is engine B of Run 1 and both seats of Runs 3a and 3b, and landing it earlier would have changed an engine mid-sample. `tools/ci.sh` passes at the new radius, including the sha-pinned tactical suite at 20 of 20 — which is not a formality: those cases were pre-registered against radius 3 and name `configs/instrument_v0.toml` by name, so a narrower candidate set failing them would have been a rules-level regression rather than a strength trade. **`configs/play_v0.toml` STAYS AT RADIUS 3, and the two configs disagree for the first time, on purpose.** That file's own invariant — play and measurement search the same way, or a measurement says nothing about play — is suspended and the suspension is written into it, because the evidence has the wrong shape to move it: Run 1 is NODE-matched, and radius 2 won it while spending 1.90x the wall-clock for 6.1% fewer nodes, so under this mode's wall-clock budget it would hold about half the nodes it had and nothing measured says the depth advantage survives the halving. Moving both files would have been the extrapolation D-190 declined to make; the time-matched SPRT that reunites them is WP-1.4's, and until D-95's movetime floor is fixed that comparison is not merely unrun but unrunnable. **Two consequences of the switch, recorded because each is a trap otherwise.** `configs/instrument_r2_v0.toml` is now value-identical to the committed config; it is kept rather than deleted because completed run reports name it by path and pin it by digest, and deleting a document that a strength claim's evidence cites is worse than leaving a redundant one. And the two WP-1.3 r2-vs-r3 arena configs are now HISTORICAL: their `engine_b` names `instrument_v0.toml`, so re-running either today is a self-match between two radius-2 configurations reporting `inconclusive_degenerate`, not the experiment it describes — a note saying so was added to each, changing no value, since the values are the experiment and reproduction goes by the recorded revision and the reports' `config_sha256` lines rather than by path (D-161) — flips when Stage 1's threat-first staged generation supersedes the radius policy as the primary candidate source (ROADMAP WP-1.5), at which point this knob becomes a config-selectable fallback and this line is history; or earlier, on a time-matched SPRT that contradicts the node-matched one.

D-195: PROCESS LAW, added to CLAUDE.md's Process section: the revision that GOVERNS a run must itself pass a fresh-context review before the first run it governs, and reviews of superseded revisions do not transfer — an amendment reopens the review, however small the diff.
